source: Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution, trans. F. G. Kenyon (1891), and Plutarch, Life of Aristides (paraphrased)
text: A voter who couldn't write once asked a stranger to scratch the name Aristides on his potsherd, because he was tired of hearing Aristides called the Just. The stranger was Aristides; he wrote it, and was ostracised.
summary: A voter who could not write asked a stranger to write Aristides’ name on a potsherd; the stranger, who was Aristides, wrote it and was ostracised.

source: Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution, trans. F. G. Kenyon (1891), and Plutarch, Life of Aristides (paraphrased)
citation: Aristotle, The Athenian Constitution 22; Plutarch, Life of Aristides 7
text: Once a year the assembly may hold an ostracism. Each citizen scratches a name on a potsherd, and if at least 6,000 votes are cast, the man named most often must leave Athens for ten years, though he keeps his property.
summary: The assembly may hold an ostracism; if at least 6,000 votes are cast, the most named man must leave Athens for ten years but keeps his property.

source: Grágás, the laws of the Icelandic Commonwealth (paraphrased)
text: Full outlawry: no one may feed, shelter or help the outlaw, nor carry him abroad, and his property is forfeit, for the rest of his life.
summary: No one may feed, shelter, help, or carry an outlaw, and his property is forfeited for life.

source: Grágás, the laws of the Icelandic Commonwealth (paraphrased)
text: Lesser outlawry: the guilty must leave Iceland within three summers and stay abroad for three years, and until a ship takes them may live safely at only three homes.
summary: A guilty person must leave Iceland within three summers, stay abroad for three years, and may live safely at only three homes until a ship takes them.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one ensnare another, putting a ban upon him, but he can not prove it, then he that ensnared him shall be put to death.
summary: This law forbids placing a ban on someone without being able to prove it, and punishes the false accuser with death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one bring an accusation against a man, and the accused go to the river and leap into the river, if he sink in the river his accuser shall take possession of his house. But if the river prove that the accused is not guilty, and he escape unhurt, then he who had brought the accusation shall be put to death, while he who leaped into the river shall take possession of the house that had belonged to his accuser.
summary: This law forbids bringing an unproven accusation involving a river trial, and punishes the losing party by forfeiture of property or death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one bring an accusation of any crime before the elders, and does not prove what he has charged, he shall, if it be a capital offense charged, be put to death.
summary: This law forbids bringing a false capital charge before the elders, and punishes the accuser with death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he satisfy the elders to impose a fine of grain or money, he shall receive the fine that the action produces.
summary: This law allows a successful accuser to collect a fine of grain or money ordered by the elders.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a judge try a case, reach a decision, and present his judgment in writing; if later error shall appear in his decision, and it be through his own fault, then he shall pay twelve times the fine set by him in the case, and he shall be publicly removed from the judge's bench, and never again shall he sit there to render judgement.
summary: This law forbids a judge from making a faulty decision through his own error, and punishes him with a fine twelve times the original amount and permanent removal from the bench.
punishment: Fine of twelve times the amount and public removal

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one steal the property of a temple or of the court, he shall be put to death, and also the one who receives the stolen thing from him shall be put to death.
summary: This law forbids stealing or receiving stolen temple or court property, and punishes both the thief and receiver with death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one buy from the son or the slave of another man, without witnesses or a contract, silver or gold, a male or female slave, an ox or a sheep, an ass or anything, or if he take it in charge, he is considered a thief and shall be put to death.
summary: This law forbids buying or taking property from another man's son or slave without witnesses or a contract, and punishes the offender as a thief with death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one steal cattle or sheep, or an ass, or a pig or a goat, if it belong to a god or to the court, the thief shall pay thirtyfold therefor; if they belonged to a freed man of the king he shall pay tenfold; if the thief has nothing with which to pay he shall be put to death.
summary: This law forbids stealing livestock, punishing temple or court thefts with a thirtyfold payment, royal property thefts with a tenfold payment, and insolvent thieves with death.
punishment: Thirtyfold or tenfold payment, or death if unable to pay

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one lose an article, and find it in the possession of another: if the person in whose possession the thing is found say "A merchant sold it to me, I paid for it before witnesses," and if the owner of the thing say, "I will bring witnesses who know my property," then shall the purchaser bring the merchant who sold it to him, and the witnesses before whom he bought it, and the owner shall bring witnesses who can identify his property. The judge shall examine their testimony--both of the witnesses before whom the price was paid, and of the witnesses who identify the lost article on oath. The merchant is then proved to be a thief and shall be put to death. The owner of the lost article receives his property, and he who bought it receives the money he paid from the estate of the merchant.
summary: If someone buys a lost article and cannot prove the merchant sold it, the merchant is executed as a thief.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the purchaser does not bring the merchant and the witnesses before whom he bought the article, but its owner bring witnesses who identify it, then the buyer is the thief and shall be put to death, and the owner receives the lost article.
summary: If a buyer cannot produce the merchant or witnesses for a disputed article, the buyer is executed as a thief.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the owner do not bring witnesses to identify the lost article, he is an evil-doer, he has traduced, and shall be put to death.
summary: If the owner fails to bring witnesses to identify a lost article, they are put to death as a false accuser.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the witnesses be not at hand, then shall the judge set a limit, at the expiration of six months. If his witnesses have not appeared within the six months, he is an evil-doer, and shall bear the fine of the pending case.
summary: If witnesses do not appear within six months, the person is branded an evil-doer and must pay the fine.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one steal the minor son of another, he shall be put to death.
summary: Anyone who steals the minor son of another person shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one take a male or female slave of the court, or a male or female slave of a freed man, outside the city gates, he shall be put to death.
summary: Anyone who takes a court or freed person's slave outside the city gates shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one receive into his house a runaway male or female slave of the court, or of a freedman, and does not bring it out at the public proclamation of the major domus, the master of the house shall be put to death.
summary: If a householder harbors a runaway slave and fails to produce them at public proclamation, they shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one find runaway male or female slaves in the open country and bring them to their masters, the master of the slaves shall pay him two shekels of silver.
summary: If anyone finds a runaway slave in the open country and returns them, the master shall pay two shekels of silver.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the slave will not give the name of the master, the finder shall bring him to the palace; a further investigation must follow, and the slave shall be returned to his master.
summary: This law forbids withholding the master's name of a found slave, and requires bringing the slave to the palace for investigation and return.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he hold the slaves in his house, and they are caught there, he shall be put to death.
summary: This law forbids harboring a slave in one's house, and punishes it with death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the slave that he caught run away from him, then shall he swear to the owners of the slave, and he is free of all blame.
summary: This law states that if a captured slave escapes, the finder is freed from blame after swearing an oath to the owners.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one break a hole into a house (break in to steal), he shall be put to death before that hole and be buried.
summary: This law forbids breaking into a house to steal, and punishes it with death by being buried before the hole.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one is committing a robbery and is caught, then he shall be put to death.
summary: This law forbids committing robbery, and punishes the caught robber with death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the robber is not caught, then shall he who was robbed claim under oath the amount of his loss; then shall the community, and . . . on whose ground and territory and in whose domain it was compensate him for the goods stolen.
summary: This law requires the local community to compensate a robbed person for their lost goods if the robber is not caught and the victim swears an oath.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If persons are stolen, then shall the community and . . . pay one mina of silver to their relatives.
summary: This law requires the community to pay one mina of silver to relatives if persons are stolen within their territory.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If fire break out in a house, and some one who comes to put it out cast his eye upon the property of the owner of the house, and take the property of the master of the house, he shall be thrown into that self-same fire.
summary: This law forbids stealing from a burning house, and punishes the thief by being thrown into the fire.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a chieftain or a man (common soldier), who has been ordered to go upon the king's highway for war does not go, but hires a mercenary, if he withholds the compensation, then shall this officer or man be put to death, and he who represented him shall take possession of his house.
summary: If a soldier avoids military service by hiring a mercenary and then withholds the mercenary's pay, he is put to death and his substitute takes his house.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a chieftain or man be caught in the misfortune of the king (captured in battle), and if his fields and garden be given to another and he take possession, if he return and reaches his place, his field and garden shall be returned to him, he shall take it over again.
summary: If a soldier captured in battle has his land given to another, his land is returned to him if he manages to return home.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a chieftain or a man be caught in the misfortune of a king, if his son is able to enter into possession, then the field and garden shall be given to him, he shall take over the fee of his father.
summary: If a soldier is captured in battle and has a son able to take possession, his land is given to his son.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If his son is still young, and can not take possession, a third of the field and garden shall be given to his mother, and she shall bring him up.
summary: If the captured soldier's son is too young, a third of the land is given to the mother to raise the child.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a chieftain or a man leave his house, garden, and field and hires it out, and some one else takes possession of his house, garden, and field and uses it for three years: if the first owner return and claims his house, garden, and field, it shall not be given to him, but he who has taken possession of it and used it shall continue to use it.
summary: If a person abandons property for three years and another uses it, the original owner cannot reclaim it upon returning.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he hire it out for one year and then return, the house, garden, and field shall be given back to him, and he shall take it over again.
summary: If property is rented out for only one year, it is returned to the owner upon their return.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a chieftain or a man is captured on the "Way of the King" (in war), and a merchant buy him free, and bring him back to his place; if he have the means in his house to buy his freedom, he shall buy himself free: if he have nothing in his house with which to buy himself free, he shall be bought free by the temple of his community; if there be nothing in the temple with which to buy him free, the court shall buy his freedom. His field, garden, and house shall not be given for the purchase of his freedom.
summary: If a captured soldier is ransomed by a merchant, he must repay the cost himself or be redeemed by the temple or court.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a . . . or a . . . enter himself as withdrawn from the "Way of the King," and send a mercenary as substitute, but withdraw him, then the . . . or . . . shall be put to death.
summary: If an official withdraws from military service, sends a substitute, and then recalls that substitute, he is put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a . . . or a . . . harm the property of a captain, injure the captain, or take away from the captain a gift presented to him by the king, then the . . . or . . . shall be put to death.
summary: If someone harms a captain's property, injures him, or takes his royal gift, they shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one buy the cattle or sheep which the king has given to chieftains from him, he loses his money.
summary: If anyone buys cattle or sheep given by the king to chieftains, the buyer loses their money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: The field, garden, and house of a chieftain, of a man, or of one subject to quit-rent, can not be sold.
summary: The field, garden, and house of a chieftain, man, or rent-payer cannot be sold.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one buy the field, garden, and house of a chieftain, man, or one subject to quit-rent, his contract tablet of sale shall be broken (declared invalid) and he loses his money. The field, garden, and house return to their owners.
summary: If anyone buys protected land or property, the sale contract is voided, the buyer loses their money, and the property returns to its owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: A chieftain, man, or one subject to quit-rent can not assign his tenure of field, house, and garden to his wife or daughter, nor can he assign it for a debt.
summary: Certain landowners cannot assign their official land, house, or garden to their wife or daughter, nor use them to pay a debt.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: He may, however, assign a field, garden, or house which he has bought, and holds as property, to his wife or daughter or give it for debt.
summary: A landowner may assign or use for debt any field, garden, or house that they personally bought and hold as private property to their wife or daughter.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: He may sell field, garden, and house to a merchant (royal agents) or to any other public official, the buyer holding field, house, and garden for its usufruct.
summary: A property holder may sell their field, garden, and house to a merchant or public official for its use.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one fence in the field, garden, and house of a chieftain, man, or one subject to quit-rent, furnishing the palings therefor; if the chieftain, man, or one subject to quit-rent return to field, garden, and house, the palings which were given to him become his property.
summary: If someone fences in another's property and the owner returns, the fencing materials become the owner's property.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one take over a field to till it, and obtain no harvest therefrom, it must be proved that he did no work on the field, and he must deliver grain, just as his neighbor raised, to the owner of the field.
summary: If a farmer fails to grow crops due to laziness, he must pay grain to the field owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he do not till the field, but let it lie fallow, he shall give grain like his neighbor's to the owner of the field, and the field which he let lie fallow he must plow and sow and return to its owner.
summary: If a farmer leaves a rented field fallow without working it, he must pay grain and return the plowed and sown field to the owner.
punishment: Give grain and return plowed field

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one take over a waste-lying field to make it arable, but is lazy, and does not make it arable, he shall plow the fallow field in the fourth year, harrow it and till it, and give it back to its owner, and for each ten gan (a measure of area) ten gur of grain shall be paid.
summary: If someone takes a waste field to farm but is lazy and fails to make it arable, they must till it and pay ten gur of grain for each ten gan.
punishment: Till the field and pay grain

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man rent his field for tillage for a fixed rental, and receive the rent of his field, but bad weather come and destroy the harvest, the injury falls upon the tiller of the soil.
summary: If a farmer rents a field for a fixed fee and bad weather ruins the harvest, the loss falls on the farmer.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he do not receive a fixed rental for his field, but lets it on half or third shares of the harvest, the grain on the field shall be divided proportionately between the tiller and the owner.
summary: If a field is rented on a sharecrop basis, the harvested grain is split proportionally between the tiller and the owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the tiller, because he did not succeed in the first year, has had the soil tilled by others, the owner may raise no objection; the field has been cultivated and he receives the harvest according to agreement.
summary: If a tiller has others work the field because he failed the first year, the owner cannot object as long as it is cultivated and he gets his share.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one owe a debt for a loan, and a storm prostrates the grain, or the harvest fail, or the grain does not grow for lack of water; in that year he need not give his creditor any grain, he washes his debt-tablet in water and pays no rent for this year.
summary: If a debtor cannot pay a grain loan due to bad weather or drought, he owes no grain for that year and washes his debt-tablet.
punishment: Exemption from payment for the year

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one take money from a merchant, and give the merchant a field tillable for corn or sesame and order him to plant corn or sesame in the field, and to harvest the crop; if the cultivator plant corn or sesame in the field, at the harvest the corn or sesame that is in the field shall belong to the owner of the field and he shall pay corn as rent, for the money he received from the merchant, and the livelihood of the cultivator shall he give to the merchant.
summary: If someone pledges a field to a merchant for money and the cultivator grows crops, the field owner takes the crop, pays rent to the owner, and provides a livelihood to the merchant.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he give a cultivated corn-field or a cultivated sesame-field, the corn or sesame in the field shall belong to the owner of the field, and he shall return the money to the merchant as rent.
summary: This law forbids keeping the crop of a rented field from the owner, and requires returning the rent money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he have no money to repay, then he shall pay in corn or sesame in place of the money as rent for what he received from the merchant, according to the royal tariff.
summary: This law allows a tenant without money to pay their field rent in corn or sesame according to the royal tariff.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the cultivator do not plant corn or sesame in the field, the debtor's contract is not weakened.
summary: This law states that failing to plant crops on a rented field does not invalidate the debtor's contract.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one be too lazy to keep his dam in proper condition, and does not so keep it; if then the dam break and all the fields be flooded, then shall he in whose dam the break occurred be sold for money, and the money shall replace the corn which he has caused to be ruined.
summary: This law forbids neglecting a dam that causes flooding, and punishes the offender by being sold into slavery to pay for the ruined crops.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he be not able to replace the corn, then he and his possessions shall be divided among the farmers whose corn he has flooded.
summary: This law requires anyone unable to replace flooded corn to have themselves and their possessions divided among the affected farmers.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one open his ditches to water his crop, but is careless, and the water flood the field of his neighbor, then he shall pay his neighbor corn for his loss.
summary: This law forbids carelessness when watering crops that floods a neighbor's field, requiring compensation in corn.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man let in the water, and the water overflow the plantation of his neighbor, he shall pay ten gur of corn for every ten gan of land.
summary: This law forbids letting water overflow a neighbor's plantation, requiring a fine of ten gur of corn for every ten gan of land.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a shepherd, without the permission of the owner of the field, and without the knowledge of the owner of the sheep, lets the sheep into a field to graze, then the owner of the field shall harvest his crop, and the shepherd, who had pastured his flock there without permission of the owner of the field, shall pay to the owner twenty gur of corn for every ten gan.
summary: This law forbids pasturing sheep on another's field without permission, requiring a payment of twenty gur of corn for every ten gan.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If after the flocks have left the pasture and been shut up in the common fold at the city gate, any shepherd let them into a field and they graze there, this shepherd shall take possession of the field which he has allowed to be grazed on, and at the harvest he must pay sixty gur of corn for every ten gan.
summary: This law forbids a shepherd from letting sheltered flocks graze in another's field, and requires him to forfeit the field and pay sixty gur of corn per ten gan at harvest.
punishment: Forfeit of field and 60 gur of corn per ten gan

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any man, without the knowledge of the owner of a garden, fell a tree in a garden he shall pay half a mina in money.
summary: This law forbids cutting down a tree in someone else's garden without their knowledge, and requires paying half a mina in money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one give over a field to a gardener, for him to plant it as a garden, if he work at it, and care for it for four years, in the fifth year the owner and the gardener shall divide it, the owner taking his part in charge.
summary: This law dictates that if a gardener tends a planted field for four years, the owner and gardener shall divide it equally in the fifth year.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the gardener has not completed the planting of the field, leaving one part unused, this shall be assigned to him as his.
summary: This law states that if a gardener leaves part of a field unplanted, that unused portion shall be assigned to the gardener.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he do not plant the field that was given over to him as a garden, if it be arable land (for corn or sesame) the gardener shall pay the owner the produce of the field for the years that he let it lie fallow, according to the product of neighboring fields, put the field in arable condition and return it to its owner.
summary: This law forbids a gardener from leaving a given garden field fallow, requiring payment of neighboring crop yields for those years, restoring the field, and returning it.
punishment: Pay produce for fallow years and restore field

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he transform waste land into arable fields and return it to its owner, the latter shall pay him for one year ten gur for ten gan.
summary: This law requires an owner to pay a gardener ten gur for ten gan for one year if the gardener transforms waste land into arable fields.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hand over his garden to a gardener to work, the gardener shall pay to its owner two-thirds of the produce of the garden, for so long as he has it in possession, and the other third shall he keep.
summary: This law mandates that a gardener managing a private garden must pay two-thirds of the produce to the owner while keeping the remaining third.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the gardener do not work in the garden and the product fall off, the gardener shall pay in proportion to other neighboring gardens.
summary: This law penalizes a gardener who fails to work the garden and causes a drop in yield by requiring compensation proportional to neighboring gardens.
punishment: Proportional payment based on neighbors' yields

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: . . . interest for the money, as much as he has received, he shall give a note therefor, and on the day, when they settle, pay to the merchant.
summary: An agent must give a note for borrowed money and repay the merchant on the settlement day.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If there are no mercantile arrangements in the place whither he went, he shall leave the entire amount of money which he received with the broker to give to the merchant.
summary: If there are no business arrangements where he goes, the agent must leave all the money with a broker to give to the merchant.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a merchant entrust money to an agent (broker) for some investment, and the broker suffer a loss in the place to which he goes, he shall make good the capital to the merchant.
summary: If an agent loses investment money on a trip, he must repay the capital to the merchant.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If, while on the journey, an enemy take away from him anything that he had, the broker shall swear by God and be free of obligation.
summary: If an enemy steals goods on the journey, the agent is freed from the obligation by swearing an oath by God.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a merchant give an agent corn, wool, oil, or any other goods to transport, the agent shall give a receipt for the amount, and compensate the merchant therefor. Then he shall obtain a receipt form the merchant for the money that he gives the merchant.
summary: An agent transporting goods must give a receipt, compensate the merchant, and obtain a receipt for any money paid back.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the agent is careless, and does not take a receipt for the money which he gave the merchant, he can not consider the unreceipted money as his own.
summary: If an agent fails to take a receipt for money given to the merchant, that unreceipted money cannot be claimed as his own.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the agent accept money from the merchant, but have a quarrel with the merchant (denying the receipt), then shall the merchant swear before God and witnesses that he has given this money to the agent, and the agent shall pay him three times the sum.
summary: If an agent denies receiving money and quarrels with the merchant, the merchant swears an oath and the agent must pay triple the sum.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the merchant cheat the agent, in that as the latter has returned to him all that had been given him, but the merchant denies the receipt of what had been returned to him, then shall this agent convict the merchant before God and the judges, and if he still deny receiving what the agent had given him shall pay six times the sum to the agent.
summary: If a merchant falsely denies receiving returned goods from an agent, he must pay six times the sum to the agent.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a tavern-keeper (feminine) does not accept corn according to gross weight in payment of drink, but takes money, and the price of the drink is less than that of the corn, she shall be convicted and thrown into the water.
summary: If a female tavern-keeper accepts money instead of corn for drinks and charges more than the value of the corn, she shall be thrown into the water.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If conspirators meet in the house of a tavern-keeper, and these conspirators are not captured and delivered to the court, the tavern-keeper shall be put to death.
summary: If conspirators meet at a tavern-keeper's house and she fails to capture and deliver them to court, she shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a "sister of a god" open a tavern, or enter a tavern to drink, then shall this woman be burned to death.
summary: If a religious sister opens or enters a tavern to drink, she shall be burned to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If an inn-keeper furnish sixty ka of usakani-drink to . . . she shall receive fifty ka of corn at the harvest.
summary: If an inn-keeper furnishes sixty ka of drink, she shall receive fifty ka of corn at the harvest.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one be on a journey and entrust silver, gold, precious stones, or any movable property to another, and wish to recover it from him; if the latter do not bring all of the property to the appointed place, but appropriate it to his own use, then shall this man, who did not bring the property to hand it over, be convicted, and he shall pay fivefold for all that had been entrusted to him.
summary: If someone entrusts property to another for a journey and the keeper appropriates it instead of returning it, he must pay fivefold its value.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one have consignment of corn or money, and he take from the granary or box without the knowledge of the owner, then shall he who took corn without the knowledge of the owner out of the granary or money out of the box be legally convicted, and repay the corn he has taken. And he shall lose whatever commission was paid to him, or due him.
summary: If someone takes corn or money from a consignment without the owner's knowledge, they must repay it and lose their commission.
punishment: Repay the corn and lose commission

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man have no claim on another for corn and money, and try to demand it by force, he shall pay one-third of a mina of silver in every case.
summary: If a man demands corn or money from someone he has no claim against by force, he must pay one-third of a mina of silver.
punishment: One-third of a mina of silver

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one have a claim for corn or money upon another and imprison him; if the prisoner die in prison a natural death, the case shall go no further.
summary: If someone imprisons another over a claim for corn or money and the prisoner dies a natural death in prison, no further legal action is taken.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the prisoner die in prison from blows or maltreatment, the master of the prisoner shall convict the merchant before the judge. If he was a free-born man, the son of the merchant shall be put to death; if it was a slave, he shall pay one-third of a mina of gold, and all that the master of the prisoner gave he shall forfeit.
summary: If a prisoner dies from mistreatment, the merchant's son is put to death if the prisoner was free-born, or a fine and forfeiture applies if a slave.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one fail to meet a claim for debt, and sell himself, his wife, his son, and daughter for money or give them away to forced labor: they shall work for three years in the house of the man who bought them, or the proprietor, and in the fourth year they shall be set free.
summary: If a debtor sells himself and his family into forced labor for a debt, they must work for three years and be freed in the fourth year.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he give a male or female slave away for forced labor, and the merchant sublease them, or sell them for money, no objection can be raised.
summary: If a slave is given for forced labor and the merchant subleases or sells them, no objection can be raised.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one fail to meet a claim for debt, and he sell the maid servant who has borne him children, for money, the money which the merchant has paid shall be repaid to him by the owner of the slave and she shall be freed.
summary: If a debtor sells a maidservant who bore him children, the owner must repay the merchant and the slave is freed.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one store corn for safe keeping in another person's house, and any harm happen to the corn in storage, or if the owner of the house open the granary and take some of the corn, or if especially he deny that the corn was stored in his house: then the owner of the corn shall claim his corn before God (on oath), and the owner of the house shall pay its owner for all of the corn that he took.
summary: If stored corn is harmed, stolen, or denied by the homeowner, the owner shall swear an oath before God and the homeowner must pay for the missing corn.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one store corn in another man's house he shall pay him storage at the rate of one gur for every five ka of corn per year.
summary: If anyone stores corn in another man's house, they must pay storage fees at a specified rate per year.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one give another silver, gold, or anything else to keep, he shall show everything to some witness, draw up a contract, and then hand it over for safe keeping.
summary: If anyone hands over valuables for safe keeping, they must show witnesses and draw up a contract.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he turn it over for safe keeping without witness or contract, and if he to whom it was given deny it, then he has no legitimate claim.
summary: If items are given for safe keeping without witnesses or a contract and the receiver denies it, the depositor has no legal claim.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one deliver silver, gold, or anything else to another for safe keeping, before a witness, but he deny it, he shall be brought before a judge, and all that he has denied he shall pay in full.
summary: If someone denies receiving property for safekeeping given before a witness, they must be brought before a judge and pay back the full amount.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one place his property with another for safe keeping, and there, either through thieves or robbers, his property and the property of the other man be lost, the owner of the house, through whose neglect the loss took place, shall compensate the owner for all that was given to him in charge. But the owner of the house shall try to follow up and recover his property, and take it away from the thief.
summary: If entrusted property is lost through thieves or robbers, the negligent homeowner must compensate the owner and try to recover the stolen items.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one who has not lost his goods state that they have been lost, and make false claims: if he claim his goods and amount of injury before God, even though he has not lost them, he shall be fully compensated for all his loss claimed. (I.e., the oath is all that is needed.)
summary: If someone makes a false claim about lost goods before God, they shall be fully compensated for the fake loss based on their oath.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one "point the finger" (slander) at a sister of a god or the wife of any one, and can not prove it, this man shall be taken before the judges and his brow shall be marked. (by cutting the skin, or perhaps hair.)
summary: If someone slanders a priestess or another man's wife and cannot prove it, they must be brought before judges and have their brow marked.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man take a woman to wife, but have no intercourse with her, this woman is no wife to him.
summary: If a man marries a woman but never has intercourse with her, she is not considered his wife.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man's wife be surprised (in flagrante delicto) with another man, both shall be tied and thrown into the water, but the husband may pardon his wife and the king his slaves.
summary: If a man's wife is caught sleeping with another man, both shall be tied and thrown into the water, unless pardoned by the husband or king.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man violate the wife (betrothed or child-wife) of another man, who has never known a man, and still lives in her father's house, and sleep with her and be surprised, this man shall be put to death, but the wife is blameless.
summary: If a man forces himself on another man's betrothed wife living in her father's house and is caught, the man shall be put to death while the wife is blameless.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man bring a charge against one's wife, but she is not surprised with another man, she must take an oath and then may return to her house.
summary: If a man accuses his wife without catching her with another man, she must take an oath and may return home.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the "finger is pointed" at a man's wife about another man, but she is not caught sleeping with the other man, she shall jump into the river for her husband.
summary: If a man's wife is accused of infidelity without proof, she must jump into the river to clear her name.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man is taken prisoner in war, and there is a sustenance in his house, but his wife leave house and court, and go to another house: because this wife did not keep her court, and went to another house, she shall be judicially condemned and thrown into the water.
summary: If a prisoner of war's wife abandons her home while food is available, she is condemned and thrown into the water.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one be captured in war and there is not sustenance in his house, if then his wife go to another house this woman shall be held blameless.
summary: If a man is captured in war and there is no food in his house, his wife may go to another house without blame.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man be taken prisoner in war and there be no sustenance in his house and his wife go to another house and bear children; and if later her husband return and come to his home: then this wife shall return to her husband, but the children follow their father.
summary: If a captive husband returns after his wife went to another house and had children, the wife returns to him while the children follow their biological father.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one leave his house, run away, and then his wife go to another house, if then he return, and wishes to take his wife back: because he fled from his home and ran away, the wife of this runaway shall not return to her husband.
summary: If a man runs away and his wife goes to another house, she does not have to return to him if he comes back.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man wish to separate from a woman who has borne him children, or from his wife who has borne him children: then he shall give that wife her dowry, and a part of the usufruct of field, garden, and property, so that she can rear her children. When she has brought up her children, a portion of all that is given to the children, equal as that of one son, shall be given to her. She may then marry the man of her heart.
summary: If a man divorces his wife who bore him children, he must provide her with her dowry and property to raise the children, after which she may remarry.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man wishes to separate from his wife who has borne him no children, he shall give her the amount of her purchase money and the dowry which she brought from her father's house, and let her go.
summary: If a man divorces his childless wife, he must pay her purchase money and dowry.
punishment: Return of purchase money and dowry

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If there was no purchase price he shall give her one mina of gold as a gift of release.
summary: If there was no purchase price for a wife, the divorcing husband must give her one mina of gold.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he be a freed man he shall give her one-third of a mina of gold.
summary: If a freed man is involved, he must pay one-third of a mina of gold.
punishment: One-third of a mina of gold

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man's wife, who lives in his house, wishes to leave it, plunges into debt, tries to ruin her house, neglects her husband, and is judicially convicted: if her husband offer her release, she may go on her way, and he gives her nothing as a gift of release. If her husband does not wish to release her, and if he take another wife, she shall remain as servant in her husband's house.
summary: If a wife neglects her home and is convicted, her husband may either divorce her without a gift or keep her as a servant while taking another wife.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a woman quarrel with her husband, and say: "You are not congenial to me," the reasons for her prejudice must be presented. If she is guiltless, and there is no fault on her part, but he leaves and neglects her, then no guilt attaches to this woman, she shall take her dowry and go back to her father's house.
summary: If an innocent wife rejects her husband and he neglects her, she may take her dowry and return to her father.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If she is not innocent, but leaves her husband, and ruins her house, neglecting her husband, this woman shall be cast into the water.
summary: If a wife is guilty of neglecting and ruining her home, she shall be cast into the water.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man take a wife and this woman give her husband a maid-servant, and she bear him children, but this man wishes to take another wife, this shall not be permitted to him; he shall not take a second wife.
summary: A man who has children by his wife's maid-servant is not permitted to take an additional wife.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man take a wife, and she bear him no children, and he intend to take another wife: if he take this second wife, and bring her into the house, this second wife shall not be allowed equality with his wife.
summary: If a man takes a second wife because the first bore no children, the second wife shall not be granted equality with the first wife.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man take a wife and she give this man a maid-servant as wife and she bear him children, and then this maid assume equality with the wife: because she has borne him children her master shall not sell her for money, but he may keep her as a slave, reckoning her among the maid-servants.
summary: If a maid-servant who bore her master children tries to claim equality with the wife, her master cannot sell her but may reduce her to a standard maid-servant.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If she have not borne him children, then her mistress may sell her for money.
summary: If a maid-servant who bore no children tries to claim equality, her mistress may sell her for money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man take a wife, and she be seized by disease, if he then desire to take a second wife he shall not put away his wife, who has been attacked by disease, but he shall keep her in the house which he has built and support her so long as she lives.
summary: If a man's wife falls ill, he must keep and support her in his house for the rest of her life and cannot divorce her to take another.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If this woman does not wish to remain in her husband's house, then he shall compensate her for the dowry that she brought with her from her father's house, and she may go.
summary: If an ill wife does not wish to stay, her husband must return her dowry and she may leave.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man give his wife a field, garden, and house and a deed therefor, if then after the death of her husband the sons raise no claim, then the mother may bequeath all to one of her sons whom she prefers, and need leave nothing to his brothers.
summary: If a widow is given property by deed and her sons do not contest it, she may leave it entirely to the son of her choice.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a woman who lived in a man's house made an agreement with her husband, that no creditor can arrest her, and has given a document therefor: if that man, before he married that woman, had a debt, the creditor can not hold the woman for it. But if the woman, before she entered the man's house, had contracted a debt, her creditor can not arrest her husband therefor.
summary: Pre-existing debts cannot be used by creditors to arrest a spouse who did not contract them.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If after the woman had entered the man's house, both contracted a debt, both must pay the merchant.
summary: If a husband and wife contract a debt together after marriage, both are liable to pay the merchant.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the wife of one man on account of another man has their mates (her husband and the other man's wife) murdered, both of them shall be impaled.
summary: If a wife causes her husband and another person's wife to be murdered for the sake of another man, both shall be impaled.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man be guilty of incest with his daughter, he shall be driven from the place (exiled).
summary: If a man commits incest with his daughter, he shall be exiled from the city.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man betroth a girl to his son, and his son have intercourse with her, but he (the father) afterward defile her, and be surprised, then he shall be bound and cast into the water (drowned).
summary: If a father has intercourse with a girl betrothed to his son and is caught, he shall be bound and drowned.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man betroth a girl to his son, but his son has not known her, and if then he defile her, he shall pay her half a gold mina, and compensate her for all that she brought out of her father's house. She may marry the man of her heart.
summary: If a man defiles the girl betrothed to his son before the son knows her, he must pay half a gold mina and her property back, and she may marry whom she pleases.
punishment: Half a gold mina and property compensation

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one be guilty of incest with his mother after his father, both shall be burned.
summary: If a man commits incest with his mother, both shall be burned.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one be surprised after his father with his chief wife, who has borne children, he shall be driven out of his father's house.
summary: If a man is found with his father's chief wife who has children, he shall be driven from the house.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one, who has brought chattels into his father-in-law's house, and has paid the purchase-money, looks for another wife, and says to his father-in-law: "I do not want your daughter," the girl's father may keep all that he had brought.
summary: If a man who paid a bride-price decides he wants another wife and rejects the daughter, the girl's father keeps all the brought goods.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man bring chattels into the house of his father-in-law, and pay the "purchase price" (for his wife): if then the father of the girl say: "I will not give you my daughter," he shall give him back all that he brought with him.
summary: If a father refuses to give his daughter to a man after receiving the purchase price, he must return everything the man brought.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man bring chattels into his father-in-law's house and pay the "purchase price," if then his friend slander him, and his father-in-law say to the young husband: "You shall not marry my daughter," the he shall give back to him undiminished all that he had brought with him; but his wife shall not be married to the friend.
summary: If a friend slanders a groom so the father-in-law rejects him, the father must return the bride-price, but the bride may not marry the friend.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man marry a woman, and she bear sons to him; if then this woman die, then shall her father have no claim on her dowry; this belongs to her sons.
summary: If a married woman with sons dies, her father has no claim to her dowry, which belongs to her sons.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man marry a woman and she bear him no sons; if then this woman die, if the "purchase price" which he had paid into the house of his father-in-law is repaid to him, her husband shall have no claim upon the dowry of this woman; it belongs to her father's house.
summary: If a childless wife dies and her purchase-price is refunded to her husband, he has no claim on her dowry, which belongs to her father's house.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If his father-in-law do not pay back to him the amount of the "purchase price" he may subtract the amount of the "Purchase price" from the dowry, and then pay the remainder to her father's house.
summary: If a father-in-law fails to repay the purchase price, the son-in-law may subtract that amount from the dowry and return the rest.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man give to one of his sons whom he prefers a field, garden, and house, and a deed therefor: if later the father die, and the brothers divide the estate, then they shall first give him the present of his father, and he shall accept it; and the rest of the paternal property shall they divide.
summary: If a father gives specific property to a preferred son by deed, that son receives it first before the remaining estate is divided among the brothers.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man take wives for his son, but take no wife for his minor son, and if then he die: if the sons divide the estate, they shall set aside besides his portion the money for the "purchase price" for the minor brother who had taken no wife as yet, and secure a wife for him.
summary: If a father dies without securing a wife for his minor son, the brothers must set aside money for his purchase price to get him a wife.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man marry a wife and she bear him children: if this wife die and he then take another wife and she bear him children: if then the father die, the sons must not partition the estate according to the mothers, they shall divide the dowries of their mothers only in this way; the paternal estate they shall divide equally with one another.
summary: When children from two different wives divide an estate after the father's death, the mothers' dowries are separated and the paternal estate is divided equally.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man wish to put his son out of his house, and declare before the judge: "I want to put my son out," then the judge shall examine into his reasons. If the son be guilty of no great fault, for which he can be rightfully put out, the father shall not put him out.
summary: If a father wants to disown his son, a judge must examine the reasons and prevent it if the son has committed no great fault.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he be guilty of a grave fault, which should rightfully deprive him of the filial relationship, the father shall forgive him the first time; but if he be guilty of a grave fault a second time the father may deprive his son of all filial relation.
summary: If a son commits a grave fault, the father must forgive him the first time, but a second grave fault allows the father to disown him.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If his wife bear sons to a man, or his maid-servant have borne sons, and the father while still living says to the children whom his maid-servant has borne: "My sons," and he count them with the sons of his wife; if then the father die, then the sons of the wife and of the maid-servant shall divide the paternal property in common. The son of the wife is to partition and choose.
summary: If a father acknowledges children born to his maid-servant as his own during his lifetime, they share the paternal property equally with the wife's sons.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If, however, the father while still living did not say to the sons of the maid-servant: "My sons," and then the father dies, then the sons of the maid-servant shall not share with the sons of the wife, but the freedom of the maid and her sons shall be granted. The sons of the wife shall have no right to enslave the sons of the maid; the wife shall take her dowry (from her father), and the gift that her husband gave her and deeded to her (separate from dowry, or the purchase-money paid her father), and live in the home of her husband: so long as she lives she shall use it, it shall not be sold for money. Whatever she leaves shall belong to her children.
summary: If a father does not acknowledge his maid-servant's children before dying, they receive freedom instead of a share of the estate.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If her husband made her no gift, she shall be compensated for her gift, and she shall receive a portion from the estate of her husband, equal to that of one child. If her sons oppress her, to force her out of the house, the judge shall examine into the matter, and if the sons are at fault the woman shall not leave her husband's house. If the woman desire to leave the house, she must leave to her sons the gift which her husband gave her, but she may take the dowry of her father's house. Then she may marry the man of her heart.
summary: It regulates inheritance and property rights for widows upon remarriage or if forced out by sons, and states the penalties or conditions for leaving.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If this woman bear sons to her second husband, in the place to which she went, and then die, her earlier and later sons shall divide the dowry between them.
summary: It states that if a remarried woman dies, her sons from both marriages shall divide her dowry.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If she bear no sons to her second husband, the sons of her first husband shall have the dowry.
summary: It states that if a remarried woman bears no sons to her second husband, the dowry goes to the sons of her first husband.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a State slave or the slave of a freed man marry the daughter of a free man, and children are born, the master of the slave shall have no right to enslave the children of the free.
summary: It forbids a slave's master from enslaving the children born from a marriage between a slave and a free man's daughter.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If, however, a State slave or the slave of a freed man marry a man's daughter, and after he marries her she bring a dowry from a father's house, if then they both enjoy it and found a household, and accumulate means, if then the slave die, then she who was free born may take her dowry, and all that her husband and she had earned; she shall divide them into two parts, one-half the master for the slave shall take, and the other half shall the free-born woman take for her children. If the free-born woman had no gift she shall take all that her husband and she had earned and divide it into two parts; and the master of the slave shall take one-half and she shall take the other for her children.
summary: It dictates how property and earnings are divided between a free-born widow and her deceased slave husband's master.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a widow, whose children are not grown, wishes to enter another house (remarry), she shall not enter it without the knowledge of the judge. If she enter another house the judge shall examine the state of the house of her first husband. Then the house of her first husband shall be entrusted to the second husband and the woman herself as managers. And a record must be made thereof. She shall keep the house in order, bring up the children, and not sell the house-hold utensils. He who buys the utensils of the children of a widow shall lose his money, and the goods shall return to their owners.
summary: It forbids a widow with young children from remarrying without judicial permission, and anyone who buys her children's household utensils loses their money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a "devoted woman" or a prostitute to whom her father has given a dowry and a deed therefor, but if in this deed it is not stated that she may bequeath it as she pleases, and has not explicitly stated that she has the right of disposal; if then her father die, then her brothers shall hold her field and garden, and give her corn, oil, and milk according to her portion, and satisfy her. If her brothers do not give her corn, oil, and milk according to her share, then her field and garden shall support her. She shall have the usufruct of field and garden and all that her father gave her so long as she lives, but she can not sell or assign it to others. Her position of inheritance belongs to her brothers.
summary: It dictates that a devoted woman or prostitute without a disposal deed receives support from her brothers from her inheritance, and cannot sell the property.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a "sister of a god," or a prostitute, receive a gift from her father, and a deed in which it has been explicitly stated that she may dispose of it as she pleases, and give her complete disposition thereof: if then her father die, then she may leave her property to whomsoever she pleases. Her brothers can raise no claim thereto.
summary: It allows a devoted woman or prostitute who received a specific disposal deed from her father to leave her property to anyone she pleases without her brothers claiming it.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a father give a present to his daughter--either marriageable or a prostitute unmarriageable)--and then die, then she is to receive a portion as a child from the paternal estate, and enjoy its usufruct so long as she lives. Her estate belongs to her brothers.
summary: If a father dies after giving a gift to his daughter, she receives a share of the estate for life, which then goes to her brothers.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a father devote a temple-maid or temple-virgin to God and give her no present: if then the father die, she shall receive the third of a child's portion from the inheritance of her father's house, and enjoy its usufruct so long as she lives. Her estate belongs to her brothers.
summary: If a father dies without giving a gift to his devoted temple-maid or virgin, she receives one-third of a child's portion for life, after which her estate goes to her brothers.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a father devote his daughter as a wife of Mardi of Babylon (as in 181), and give her no present, nor a deed; if then her father die, then shall she receive one-third of her portion as a child of her father's house from her brothers, but Marduk may leave her estate to whomsoever she wishes.
summary: If a father dies without giving a gift or deed to his daughter devoted to Marduk, she receives one-third of a child's portion from her brothers, and Marduk may leave her estate to her chosen heir.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man give his daughter by a concubine a dowry, and a husband, and a deed; if then her father die, she shall receive no portion from the paternal estate.
summary: If a man gives a dowry and husband to his daughter by a concubine, she receives no portion of his paternal estate upon his death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man do not give a dowry to his daughter by a concubine, and no husband; if then her father die, her brother shall give her a dowry according to her father's wealth and secure a husband for her.
summary: If a man dies without giving a dowry or husband to his daughter by a concubine, her brother must provide her with both based on the father's wealth.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man adopt a child and to his name as son, and rear him, this grown son can not be demanded back again.
summary: If a man adopts and rears a child as his son, that grown son cannot be reclaimed.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man adopt a son, and if after he has taken him he injure his foster father and mother, then this adopted son shall return to his father's house.
summary: If an adopted son injures his foster parents, he must return to his biological father's house.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: The son of a paramour in the palace service, or of a prostitute, can not be demanded back.
summary: The son of a palace paramour or prostitute cannot be demanded back.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If an artizan has undertaken to rear a child and teaches him his craft, he can not be demanded back.
summary: If an artisan adopts and teaches a child a craft, the child cannot be reclaimed.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he has not taught him his craft, this adopted son may return to his father's house.
summary: If an artisan fails to teach his adopted child his craft, the child may return to his biological father's house.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man does not maintain a child that he has adopted as a son and reared with his other children, then his adopted son may return to his father's house.
summary: If an adopter fails to maintain an adopted child along with his other children, the child may return to his father's house.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man, who had adopted a son and reared him, founded a household, and had children, wish to put this adopted son out, then this son shall not simply go his way. His adoptive father shall give him of his wealth one-third of a child's portion, and then he may go. He shall not give him of the field, garden, and house.
summary: If an adopter has his own children and wishes to dismiss an adopted son, he must give him one-third of a child's portion of his wealth excluding fields, gardens, and houses.
punishment: One-third of a child's portion of wealth

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a son of a paramour or a prostitute say to his adoptive father or mother: "You are not my father, or my mother," his tongue shall be cut off.
summary: If an adopted son of a prostitute or paramour denies his adoptive parents, his tongue shall be cut off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the son of a paramour or a prostitute desire his father's house, and desert his adoptive father and adoptive mother, and goes to his father's house, then shall his eye be put out.
summary: If an adopted son of a prostitute or paramour deserts his adoptive parents for his natural father's house, his eye shall be put out.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man give his child to a nurse and the child die in her hands, but the nurse unbeknown to the father and mother nurse another child, then they shall convict her of having nursed another child without the knowledge of the father and mother and her breasts shall be cut off.
summary: If a nurse secretly substitutes another child after a baby dies in her care, her breasts shall be cut off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a son strike his father, his hands shall be hewn off.
summary: If a son strikes his father, his hands shall be hewn off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out.
summary: If a man blinds another man, his own eye will be put out.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he break another man's bone, his bone shall be broken.
summary: If a man breaks another man's bone, his own bone will be broken.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he put out the eye of a freed man, or break the bone of a freed man, he shall pay one gold mina.
summary: If a man blinds or breaks the bone of a freed man, he must pay one gold mina.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he put out the eye of a man's slave, or break the bone of a man's slave, he shall pay one-half of its value.
summary: If a man blinds or breaks the bone of another person's slave, he must pay half the slave's value.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man knock out the teeth of his equal, his teeth shall be knocked out.
summary: If a man knocks out the tooth of his equal, his own tooth will be knocked out.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he knock out the teeth of a freed man, he shall pay one-third of a gold mina.
summary: If a man knocks out the tooth of a freed man, he must pay one-third of a gold mina.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one strike the body of a man higher in rank than he, he shall receive sixty blows with an ox-whip in public.
summary: If a man strikes someone of higher rank, he will be whipped publicly with sixty blows.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a free-born man strike the body of another free-born man or equal rank, he shall pay one gold mina.
summary: If a free-born man strikes another free-born man of equal rank, he must pay one gold mina.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a freed man strike the body of another freed man, he shall pay ten shekels in money.
summary: If a freed man strikes another freed man, he must pay ten shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the slave of a freed man strike the body of a freed man, his ear shall be cut off.
summary: If a freed man's slave strikes a freed man, the slave's ear is cut off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If during a quarrel one man strike another and wound him, then he shall swear, "I did not injure him wittingly," and pay the physicians.
summary: If a man wounds another in a quarrel, he must swear he did not do it on purpose and pay the doctor.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the man die of his wound, he shall swear similarly, and if he (the deceased) was a free-born man, he shall pay half a mina in money.
summary: If the wounded man dies, the striker must swear an oath and pay half a mina if the victim was free-born.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he was a freed man, he shall pay one-third of a mina.
summary: If the deceased victim was a freed man, the striker must pay one-third of a mina.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man strike a free-born woman so that she lose her unborn child, he shall pay ten shekels for her loss.
summary: If a man strikes a free-born woman and causes her to lose her unborn child, he must pay ten shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the woman die, his daughter shall be put to death.
summary: If the woman dies from the blow, the striker's daughter shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a woman of the free class lose her child by a blow, he shall pay five shekels in money.
summary: If a woman of the free class loses her child due to a blow, the striker must pay five shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If this woman die, he shall pay half a mina.
summary: If a man causes a free woman's death, he must pay half a mina of silver.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he strike the maid-servant of a man, and she lose her child, he shall pay two shekels in money.
summary: If a man strikes another man's maid-servant and causes her to lose her child, he must pay two shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If this maid-servant die, he shall pay one-third of a mina.
summary: If a maid-servant dies from being struck, the perpetrator must pay one-third of a mina.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a physician make a large incision with an operating knife and cure it, or if he open a tumor (over the eye) with an operating knife, and saves the eye, he shall receive ten shekels in money.
summary: If a physician successfully performs a major operation or saves an eye, he receives ten shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the patient be a freed man, he receives five shekels.
summary: If the patient is a freed man, the physician receives five shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he be the slave of some one, his owner shall give the physician two shekels.
summary: If the patient is a slave, the owner must pay the physician two shekels.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a physician make a large incision with the operating knife, and kill him, or open a tumor with the operating knife, and cut out the eye, his hands shall be cut off.
summary: If a physician kills a patient during surgery or destroys their eye, his hands shall be cut off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a physician make a large incision in the slave of a freed man, and kill him, he shall replace the slave with another slave.
summary: If a physician kills a slave during surgery, he must replace the slave with another slave.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he had opened a tumor with the operating knife, and put out his eye, he shall pay half his value.
summary: This law forbids a physician from ruining a patient's eye during surgery, and requires them to pay half the patient's value in compensation.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a physician heal the broken bone or diseased soft part of a man, the patient shall pay the physician five shekels in money.
summary: This law requires a patient who is a free man to pay a physician five shekels of silver for healing a broken bone or diseased soft part.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he were a freed man he shall pay three shekels.
summary: This law requires a freed man to pay a physician three shekels for medical treatment.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he were a slave his owner shall pay the physician two shekels.
summary: This law requires the owner of a slave to pay a physician two shekels for medical treatment.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a veterinary surgeon perform a serious operation on an ass or an ox, and cure it, the owner shall pay the surgeon one-sixth of a shekel as a fee.
summary: This law requires the owner of an ass or an ox to pay a veterinary surgeon one-sixth of a shekel for a successful serious operation.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he perform a serious operation on an ass or ox, and kill it, he shall pay the owner one-fourth of its value.
summary: This law forbids a veterinary surgeon from killing an ass or ox during an operation, and requires them to pay one-fourth of its value to the owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a barber, without the knowledge of his master, cut the sign of a slave on a slave not to be sold, the hands of this barber shall be cut off.
summary: This law forbids a barber from cutting a slave's identification mark without the master's knowledge, and requires that the barber's hands be cut off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one deceive a barber, and have him mark a slave not for sale with the sign of a slave, he shall be put to death, and buried in his house. The barber shall swear: "I did not mark him wittingly," and shall be guiltless.
summary: This law forbids anyone from deceiving a barber into marking a non-saleable slave, and punishes the deceiver with death and burial in their house while the innocent barber goes free after swearing an oath.
punishment: Death and burial in his house

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a builder build a house for some one and complete it, he shall give him a fee of two shekels in money for each sar of surface.
summary: If a builder completes a house, the owner must pay a fee of two shekels per sar of surface.
punishment: Fee of two shekels per sar

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a builder build a house for some one, and does not construct it properly, and the house which he built fall in and kill its owner, then that builder shall be put to death.
summary: If a poorly built house collapses and kills the owner, the builder shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If it kill the son of the owner the son of that builder shall be put to death.
summary: If a collapsing house kills the owner's son, the builder's son shall be put to death.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If it kill a slave of the owner, then he shall pay slave for slave to the owner of the house.
summary: If a collapsing house kills a slave, the builder must pay slave for slave to the owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If it ruin goods, he shall make compensation for all that has been ruined, and inasmuch as he did not construct properly this house which he built and it fell, he shall re-erect the house from his own means.
summary: If a collapsing house ruins goods, the builder must compensate for all ruined goods and rebuild the house from his own funds.
punishment: Compensation and rebuilding at own expense

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a builder build a house for some one, even though he has not yet completed it; if then the walls seem toppling, the builder must make the walls solid from his own means.
summary: If a builder's uncompleted walls begin to topple, the builder must reinforce them using his own means.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a shipbuilder build a boat of sixty gur for a man, he shall pay him a fee of two shekels in money.
summary: If a shipbuilder builds a sixty gur boat, he shall be paid a fee of two shekels in money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a shipbuilder build a boat for some one, and do not make it tight, if during that same year that boat is sent away and suffers injury, the shipbuilder shall take the boat apart and put it together tight at his own expense. The tight boat he shall give to the boat owner.
summary: If a leaky boat built by a shipbuilder is injured in the same year, the shipbuilder must dismantle and rebuild it tightly at his own expense.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man rent his boat to a sailor, and the sailor is careless, and the boat is wrecked or goes aground, the sailor shall give the owner of the boat another boat as compensation.
summary: If a careless sailor wrecks a rented boat, he must provide the owner with a replacement boat.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man hire a sailor and his boat, and provide it with corn, clothing, oil and dates, and other things of the kind needed for fitting it: if the sailor is careless, the boat is wrecked, and its contents ruined, then the sailor shall compensate for the boat which was wrecked and all in it that he ruined.
summary: If a careless sailor wrecks a hired boat and ruins its cargo, he must pay compensation for both the boat and the ruined contents.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a sailor wreck any one's ship, but saves it, he shall pay the half of its value in money.
summary: If a sailor wrecks a ship but manages to save it, he must pay half of its value in money.
punishment: Half the ship's value in money

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man hire a sailor, he shall pay him six gur of corn per year.
