summary: If a man hires a sailor, he must pay him six gur of corn per year.
punishment: Six gur of corn per year

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a merchantman run against a ferryboat, and wreck it, the master of the ship that was wrecked shall seek justice before God; the master of the merchantman, which wrecked the ferryboat, must compensate the owner for the boat and all that he ruined.
summary: If a merchant ship wrecks a ferryboat, the master of the wrecked boat must seek justice before God while the master of the merchant ship must compensate the owner for the boat and lost goods.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one impresses an ox for forced labor, he shall pay one-third of a mina in money.
summary: If anyone wrongfully seizes an ox for forced labor, he must pay one-third of a mina in money.
punishment: One-third of a mina in money

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire oxen for a year, he shall pay four gur of corn for plow-oxen.
summary: If anyone hires plow-oxen for a year, he must pay four gur of corn.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: As rent of herd cattle he shall pay three gur of corn to the owner.
summary: As rent for herd cattle, a person must pay three gur of corn to the owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire an ox or an ass, and a lion kill it in the field, the loss is upon its owner.
summary: If a hired animal is killed by a lion in the field, the owner must bear the loss.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire oxen, and kill them by bad treatment or blows, he shall compensate the owner, oxen for oxen.
summary: If someone kills a hired ox through bad treatment or blows, they must replace it with another ox.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a man hire an ox, and he break its leg or cut the ligament of its neck, he shall compensate the owner with ox for ox.
summary: If someone breaks a hired ox's leg or cuts its neck ligament, they must replace it with another ox.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire an ox, and put out its eye, he shall pay the owner one-half of its value.
summary: If someone blinds a hired ox's eye, they must pay the owner half its value.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire an ox, and break off a horn, or cut off its tail, or hurt its muzzle, he shall pay one-fourth of its value in money.
summary: If someone breaks a hired ox's horn, cuts its tail, or hurts its muzzle, they must pay one-fourth of its value.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire an ox, and God strike it that it die, the man who hired it shall swear by God and be considered guiltless.
summary: If a hired ox dies by divine act, the hirer can swear by God and be declared innocent.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If while an ox is passing on the street (market) some one push it, and kill it, the owner can set up no claim in the suit (against the hirer).
summary: If someone pushes a passing ox in the street and kills it, the owner cannot sue the hirer.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If an ox be a goring ox, and it shown that he is a gorer, and he do not bind his horns, or fasten the ox up, and the ox gore a free-born man and kill him, the owner shall pay one-half a mina in money.
summary: If an owner knows their ox is a gorer and fails to secure it, and it kills a free-born man, the owner must pay half a mina of silver.
punishment: Pay one-half a mina in money

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he kill a man's slave, he shall pay one-third of a mina.
summary: If someone kills another person's slave, they must pay one-third of a mina.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one agree with another to tend his field, give him seed, entrust a yoke of oxen to him, and bind him to cultivate the field, if he steal the corn or plants, and take them for himself, his hands shall be hewn off.
summary: If a hired field tender steals the corn or plants for themselves, their hands shall be cut off.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he take the seed-corn for himself, and do not use the yoke of oxen, he shall compensate him for the amount of the seed-corn.
summary: If someone takes the seed-corn for themselves instead of using the oxen, they must compensate the owner for the seed.
punishment: Compensate for the amount of the seed-corn

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he sublet the man's yoke of oxen or steal the seed-corn, planting nothing in the field, he shall be convicted, and for each one hundred gan he shall pay sixty gur of corn.
summary: If someone sublets the oxen or steals the seed-corn without planting, they must pay sixty gur of corn per hundred gan upon conviction.
punishment: Sixty gur of corn per hundred gan

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If his community will not pay for him, then he shall be placed in that field with the cattle (at work).
summary: If the community refuses to pay for someone, that person shall be put to work in the field with the cattle.
punishment: Placed in that field with the cattle at work

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a field laborer, he shall pay him eight gur of corn per year.
summary: If someone hires a field laborer, they must pay them eight gur of corn per year.
punishment: Eight gur of corn per year

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire an ox-driver, he shall pay him six gur of corn per year.
summary: If someone hires an ox-driver, they must pay them six gur of corn per year.
punishment: Six gur of corn per year

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one steal a water-wheel from the field, he shall pay five shekels in money to its owner.
summary: If someone steals a water-wheel from a field, they must pay five shekels in money to the owner.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one steal a shadduf (used to draw water from the river or canal) or a plow, he shall pay three shekels in money.
summary: If anyone steals a water-drawing device or a plow, they must pay three shekels in money.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a herdsman for cattle or sheep, he shall pay him eight gur of corn per annum.
summary: If anyone hires a herdsman for cattle or sheep, they shall pay him eight gur of corn per year.
punishment: Payment of eight gur of corn

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one, a cow or a sheep . . .
summary: If anyone [damages or loses] a cow or a sheep.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he kill the cattle or sheep that were given to him, he shall compensate the owner with cattle for cattle and sheep for sheep.
summary: If anyone kills the cattle or sheep given to them, they must compensate the owner with equivalent cattle and sheep.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a herdsman, to whom cattle or sheep have been entrusted for watching over, and who has received his wages as agreed upon, and is satisfied, diminish the number of the cattle or sheep, or make the increase by birth less, he shall make good the increase or profit which was lost in the terms of settlement.
summary: If a paid and satisfied herdsman diminishes the number of animals or their birth increase, he must make good the lost profit.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a herdsman, to whose care cattle or sheep have been entrusted, be guilty of fraud and make false returns of the natural increase, or sell them for money, then shall he be convicted and pay the owner ten times the loss.
summary: If a herdsman commits fraud regarding the increase of animals or sells them, he shall pay the owner ten times the loss.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the animal be killed in the stable by God ( an accident), or if a lion kill it, the herdsman shall declare his innocence before God, and the owner bears the accident in the stable.
summary: If an animal is killed by an accident or a lion in the stable, the herdsman swears his innocence before God and the owner bears the loss.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If the herdsman overlook something, and an accident happen in the stable, then the herdsman is at fault for the accident which he has caused in the stable, and he must compensate the owner for the cattle or sheep.
summary: If a herdsman is careless and an accident happens in the stable, he is at fault and must compensate the owner for the animals.
punishment: Compensate the owner for the animals

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire an ox for threshing, the amount of the hire is twenty ka of corn.
summary: This law sets the standard hire price for an ox used in threshing at twenty ka of corn.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he hire an ass for threshing, the hire is twenty ka of corn.
summary: This law sets the standard hire price for an ass used in threshing at twenty ka of corn.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he hire a young animal for threshing, the hire is ten ka of corn.
summary: This law sets the standard hire price for a young animal used in threshing at ten ka of corn.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire oxen, cart and driver, he shall pay one hundred and eighty ka of corn per day.
summary: This law sets the daily hire price for oxen, a cart, and a driver at one hundred and eighty ka of corn.
punishment: One hundred and eighty ka of corn per day

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a cart alone, he shall pay forty ka of corn per day.
summary: This law sets the daily hire price for a cart alone at forty ka of corn.
punishment: Forty ka of corn per day

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a day laborer, he shall pay him from the New Year until the fifth month (April to August, when days are long and the work hard) six gerahs in money per day; from the sixth month to the end of the year he shall give him five gerahs per day.
summary: This law sets the daily wage for a day laborer at six gerahs from the New Year to the fifth month, and five gerahs for the rest of the year.
punishment: Five to six gerahs per day

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a skilled artizan, he shall pay as wages of the . . . five gerahs, as wages of the potter five gerahs, of a tailor five gerahs, of . . . gerahs, . . . of a ropemaker four gerahs, of . . .. gerahs, of a mason . . . gerahs per day.
summary: This law sets the specific daily wages for various skilled artisans and craftsmen.
punishment: Four to five gerahs per day

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a ferryboat, he shall pay three gerahs in money per day.
summary: This law sets the daily hire price for a ferryboat at three gerahs in money.
punishment: Three gerahs in money per day

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If he hire a freight-boat, he shall pay two and one-half gerahs per day.
summary: A person hiring a freight-boat must pay two and one-half gerahs per day.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one hire a ship of sixty gur, he shall pay one-sixth of a shekel in money as its hire per day.
summary: A person hiring a ship of sixty gur must pay one-sixth of a shekel per day.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one buy a male or female slave, and before a month has elapsed the benu-disease be developed, he shall return the slave to the seller, and receive the money which he had paid.
summary: If a buyer purchases a slave and the slave develops benu-disease within a month, the buyer must return the slave and receive a refund of the purchase price.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If any one buy a male or female slave, and a third party claim it, the seller is liable for the claim.
summary: If a third party claims a slave bought by a buyer, the seller is liable for the claim.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If while in a foreign country a man buy a male or female slave belonging to another of his own country; if when he return home the owner of the male or female slave recognize it: if the male or female slave be a native of the country, he shall give them back without any money.
summary: If a man buys a slave of his own country while abroad and the slave is native to the foreign country, he must return the slave without payment.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If they are from another country, the buyer shall declare the amount of money paid therefor to the merchant, and keep the male or female slave.
summary: If a man buys a slave of another country while abroad, he must declare the purchase price to the merchant and keep the slave.

source: Code of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King
text: If a slave say to his master: "You are not my master," if they convict him his master shall cut off his ear.
summary: If a slave claims he is not his master, the master may cut off his ear.

source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Spartans must speak briefly, packing much meaning into few words; idle chatter is shameful.
summary: Spartans must speak briefly; idle chatter is shameful.

source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: The roof of every house may be shaped with the axe alone, and its doors with the saw alone, so that no one builds anything fancy.
summary: The law forbids building roofs with anything but an axe and doors with anything but a saw, preventing fancy construction.

source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Every man must eat at the common mess and bring each month a bushel of barley meal, eight gallons of wine, five pounds of cheese, two and a half pounds of figs and a little money for meat or fish. Dining richly at home is forbidden.
summary: The law requires men to eat at the common mess and provide monthly food supplies, forbidding rich dining at home.

source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Citizens may not travel abroad as they please, and strangers with no useful business are sent away, so that foreign habits do not spoil the city.
summary: The law prohibits citizens from traveling abroad freely and expels strangers without useful business.

source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Gold and silver are banned; only iron money may be used, so heavy and worth so little that ten minas need a storeroom to hold them and a yoke of oxen to move them.
summary: The law bans gold and silver, allowing only iron money for transactions.

source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: No law may be written down: the laws must live in the citizens' habits and training instead.
summary: The law states that no law may be written down; laws must exist only in citizens' habits and training.

source: The Great Qing Code, trans. G. T. Staunton (1810) (paraphrased)
text: Perpetual banishment sends the guilty 2,000, 2,500 or 3,000 li from home, about 1,000 to 1,500 kilometres, after 100 blows of the bamboo.
summary: Perpetual banishment sends the guilty 2,000 to 3,000 li (about 1,000–1,500 km) from home after 100 blows of the bamboo.

source: The Great Qing Code, trans. G. T. Staunton (1810) (paraphrased)
text: The code knows five punishments: the light bamboo, the heavy bamboo, banishment for one to three years, perpetual banishment of 2,000 to 3,000 li, and death.
summary: The code lists five punishments: light bamboo, heavy bamboo, banishment for one to three years, perpetual banishment of 2,000–3,000 li, and death.

source: The Great Qing Code, trans. G. T. Staunton (1810) (paraphrased)
citation: Qing Code, the statute on gambling
text: Gamblers receive 80 blows of the bamboo, and every stake on the table is forfeit to the government.
summary: Gamblers receive 80 blows of the bamboo and all stakes on the table are forfeited to the government.
punishment: 80 blows of bamboo and forfeiture of stakes

source: The Great Qing Code, trans. G. T. Staunton (1810) (paraphrased)
citation: Qing Code, the rule on complaints of abuse
text: Abusive language can be punished only if the person abused heard it, and complains of it themselves.
summary: Abusive language can be punished only if the abused person heard it and complains themselves.

source: The Great Qing Code, trans. G. T. Staunton (1810) (paraphrased)
citation: Qing Code, the statute on abusive language
text: Whoever abuses another person receives 10 blows of the light bamboo; when two people trade abuse, each receives 10.
summary: Abusing another person causes 10 blows of light bamboo; mutual abuse gives each 10 blows.

source: The Great Qing Code, trans. G. T. Staunton (1810) (paraphrased)
citation: Qing Code, the statute on theft
text: Theft is punished by the value of what was taken: 60 blows of the bamboo for a tael or less, rising step by step to 100 blows and perpetual banishment of 3,000 li at 100 taels, and strangling at 120 taels or more. A first-time thief is also tattooed on the arm.
summary: Theft is punished by blows of bamboo proportional to value, up to 120 blows and strangling for large thefts, with banishment for 100 taels, and first-time thieves get a tattoo.

source: Roman exile, as described by Cicero, Livy and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: A condemned citizen who flees is forbidden fire and water anywhere in Roman lands, so that no one may shelter him: exile, in all but name.
summary: A condemned citizen who flees is forbidden fire and water anywhere in Roman lands, effectively exiling them.

source: Roman exile, as described by Cicero, Livy and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: Relegation sends someone to a fixed place but leaves them their property and citizenship: Augustus relegated the poet Ovid to Tomis, on the Black Sea, for what Ovid called a poem and a mistake.
summary: Relegation sends a person to a fixed place while keeping their property and citizenship.

source: Rome's laws against luxury, as reported by Livy, Macrobius and Aulus Gellius (paraphrased)
text: No advocate may take money or gifts for pleading someone's case.
summary: The law forbids advocates from accepting money or gifts for pleading a case.

source: Rome's laws against luxury, as reported by Livy, Macrobius and Aulus Gellius (paraphrased)
citation: Lex Fannia (161 BC), in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 2.24
text: A dinner may cost no more than a hundred asses on certain festival days, thirty on some others, and ten on ordinary days.
summary: The law limits the cost of a dinner to no more than a hundred asses on certain festival days, thirty on others, and ten on ordinary days.

source: Rome's laws against luxury, as reported by Livy, Macrobius and Aulus Gellius (paraphrased)
citation: Lex Licinia, in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 2.24
text: On an ordinary day a household may serve no more than three pounds of fresh meat and one pound of salted meat, though fruit and vegetables are unlimited.
summary: The law limits a household to no more than three pounds of fresh meat and one pound of salted meat on an ordinary day, with unlimited fruit and vegetables.

source: Rome's laws against luxury, as reported by Livy, Macrobius and Aulus Gellius (paraphrased)
citation: Lex Orchia (181 BC), in Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.17
text: The number of guests anyone may invite to dinner is limited by law.
summary: Limits the number of guests one may invite to dinner.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one be summoned before the "Thing" by the king's law, and do not come he shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings (solid)).
summary: If summoned before the "Thing" by the king's law and one does not attend, one is sentenced to 600 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But he who summons another, and does not come himself, shall, if a lawful impediment have not delayed him, be sentenced to 15 shillings, to be paid to him whom he summoned.
summary: If one summons another and does not attend, one must pay 15 shillings to the summoned person.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: And he who summons another shall walk with witnesses to the home of that man, and, if he be not at home, shall bid the wife or any one of the family to make known to him that he has been summoned to court.
summary: When summoning another, one must walk with witnesses to that person's home and, if absent, have the wife or a family member inform them of the summons.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he be occupied in the king's service he can not summon him.
summary: If one is occupied in the king's service, one cannot summon another.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he shall be inside the hundred seeing about his own affairs, he can summon him in the manner explained above.
summary: If one is inside the hundred attending to his own affairs, one may summon another as described above.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one steal a sucking pig, and it be proved against him, he shall be sentenced to 120 denars, which make three shillings.
summary: If one steals a sucking pig and is proven guilty, one is sentenced to 120 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one steal a pig that can live without its mother, and it be proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 40 denars-that is, 1 shilling.
summary: If one steals a pig that can live without its mother and is proven guilty, one is sentenced to 40 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one steal 25 sheep where there were no more in that flock, and it be proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 2500 denars-that is, 62 shillings.
summary: Stealing 25 sheep from a flock where none remain results in a fine of 2500 denars (62 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one steal that bull which rules the herd and never has been yoked, he shall be sentenced to 1800 denars, which make 45 shillings.
summary: Stealing the bull that leads the herd and has never been yoked results in a fine of 1800 denars (45 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if that bull is used for the coves of three villages in common, he who stole him shall be sentenced to three times 45 shillings.
summary: Stealing a bull used for the common use of three villages results in a fine of three times 45 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one steal a bull belonging to the king he shall be sentenced to 3600 denars, which make 90 shillings.
summary: Stealing a bull belonging to the king results in a fine of 3600 denars (90 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one finds cattle, or a horse, or flocks of any kind in his crops, he shall not at all mutilate them.
summary: Finding cattle, a horse, or flocks in one's crops is prohibited from mutilating them.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If he do this and confess it, he shall restore the worth of the animal in place of it, and shall himself keep the mutilated one.
summary: If one mutilates found animals and confesses, they must restore the animal's value and keep the mutilated one.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he have not confessed it, and it have been proved on him, he shall be sentenced, besides the value of the animal and the fines for delay, to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings.
summary: If one mutilates found animals without confessing and is proven, they must pay the animal's value, delay fines, and an additional 600 denars (15 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any freeman steal, outside of the house, something worth 2 denars, he shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings.
summary: A freeman stealing something worth 2 denars outside a house is fined 600 denars (15 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he steal, outside of the house, something worth 40 denars, and it be proved on him, he shall be sentenced, besides the amount and the fines for delay, to 1400 denars, which make 35 shillings.
summary: A person who steals an item worth 40 denars outside a house must pay 1400 denars (35 shillings) in addition to the value of the item and delay fines.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If a freeman break into a house and steal something worth 2 denars, and it be proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 15 shillings
summary: A freeman who breaks into a house and steals an item worth 2 denars must pay 15 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he shall have stolen something worth more than 5 denars, and it have been proved on him, he shall be sentenced, besides the worth of the object and the fines for delay, to 1400 denars, which make 35 shillings.
summary: A person who steals an item worth more than 5 denars must pay 1400 denars (35 shillings) in addition to the value of the item and delay fines.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he have broken, or tampered with, the lock, and thus have entered the house and stolen anything from it, he shall be sentenced, besides the worth of the object and the fines for delay, to 1800 denars, which make 45 shillings.
summary: A person who breaks or tampers with a lock to enter a house and steal any item must pay 1800 denars (45 shillings) in addition to the value of the item and delay fines.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: And if he have taken nothing, or have escaped by flight, he shall, for the housebreaking alone, be sentenced to 1200 denars, which make 30 shillings.
summary: A person who takes nothing or escapes after breaking into a house must pay 1200 denars (30 shillings) for the housebreaking alone.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If a slave steal, outside of the house, something worth two denars, he shall, besides paying the worth of the object and the fines for delay, be stretched out and receive 120 blows.
summary: A slave who steals an item worth 2 denars outside a house must pay the value of the item, delay fines, and receive 120 blows.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he steal something worth 40 denars, he shall either be castrated or pay 6 shillings. But the lord of the slave who committed the theft shall restore to the plaintiff the worth of the object and the fines for delay.
summary: A slave who steals an item worth 40 denars may be castrated or pay 6 shillings; the slave’s lord must reimburse the plaintiff the value of the item and delay fines.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If three men carry off a free born girl, they shall be compelled to pay 30 shillings.
summary: Three men who abduct a free-born girl must pay 30 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If there are more than three, each one shall pay 5 shillings.
summary: If more than three people are involved, each must pay five shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: Those who shall have been present with boats shall be sentenced to three shillings.
summary: Anyone present with boats must pay three shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But those who commit rape shall be compelled to pay 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: Rape offenders must pay 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if they have carried off that girl from behind lock and key, or from the spinning room, they shall be sentenced to the above price and penalty.
summary: If a girl is carried off from behind lock and key or from the spinning room, the offender pays the same fine as for rape.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if the girl who is carried off be under the king's protection, then the "frith" (peace-money) shall be 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: If a girl under the king's protection is carried off, the offender pays 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if a bondsman of the king, or a leet, should carry off a free woman, he shall be sentenced to death.
summary: A bondsman or leet who carries off a free woman is sentenced to death.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if a free woman have followed a slave of her own will, she shall lose her freedom.
summary: A free woman who follows a slave of her own will loses her freedom.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If a freeborn man shall have taken an alien bondswoman, he shall suffer similarly.
summary: A freeborn man who takes an alien bondswoman suffers the same penalty as the free woman.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any body take an alien spouse and join her to himself in matrimony, he shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: A person who marries an alien spouse must pay 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have assaulted and plundered a free man, and it be proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: A person who assaults and plunders a free man must pay 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If a Roman have plundered a Salian Frank, the above law shall be observed.
summary: If a Roman plunders a Salian Frank, the same fine of 2500 denars (63 shillings) applies.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if a Frank have plundered a Roman, he shall be sentenced to 35 shillings.
summary: If a Frank plunders a Roman, the offender must pay 35 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man should wish to migrate, and has permission from the king, and shall have shown this in the public "Thing;" whoever, contrary to the decree of the king, shall presume to oppose him, shall be sentenced to 8000 denars, which make 200 shillings.
summary: A man who opposes a king‑approved migration must pay 8000 denars (200 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one shall set fire to a house in which men were sleeping, as many freemen as were in it can make complaint before the " Thing; " and if any one shall have been burned in it, the incendiary shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: A person who sets fire to a house where men are sleeping must pay 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have wished to kill another person, and the blow have missed, he on whom it was proved shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: A person who attempts to kill another but misses must pay 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any person have wished to strike another with a poisoned arrow, and the arrow have glanced aside, and it shall be proved on him; he shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: A person who attempts to kill another with a poisoned arrow that misses must pay 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any person strike another on the head so that the brain appears, and the three bones which lie above the brain shall project, he shall be sentenced to 1200 denars, which make 30 shillings.
summary: Striking another on the head so that the brain appears and the three bones above the brain project results in a sentence of 1200 denars (30 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if it shall have been between the ribs or in the stomach, so that the wound appears and reaches to the entrails, he shall be sentenced to 1200 denars-which make 30 shillings-besides five shillings for the physician's pay.
summary: Striking between the ribs or in the stomach so that the wound reaches the entrails results in a sentence of 1200 denars (30 shillings) plus five shillings for the physician's pay.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one shall have struck a man so that blood falls to the floor, and it be proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings.
summary: Striking a man so that blood falls to the floor, if proven, results in a sentence of 600 denars (15 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if a freeman strike a freeman with his fist so that blood does not flow, he shall be sentenced for each blow-up to 3 blows-to 120 denars, which make 3 shillings.
summary: A freeman striking a freeman with his fist so that blood does not flow results in a sentence of 3 blows to 120 denars (3 shillings) for each blow.
punishment: 3 blows to 120 denars (3 shillings) per blow

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one, before the king, accuse an innocent man who is absent, he shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: Accusing an innocent absent man before the king results in a sentence of 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have given herbs to another so that he die, he shall be sentenced to 200 shillings (or shall surely be given over to fire).
summary: Giving herbs to another so that he dies results in a sentence of 200 shillings or execution by fire.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any person have bewitched another, and he who was thus treated shall escape, the author of the crime, who is proved to have committed it, shall be sentenced to 2500 denars, which make 63 shillings.
summary: Bewitching another and the victim escapes, if proven, results in a sentence of 2500 denars (63 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have slain a boy under 10 years-up to the end of the tenth-and it shall have been proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 24000 denars, which make 600 shillings.
summary: Slaying a boy under 10 years old results in a sentence of 24000 denars (600 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have hit a free woman who is pregnant and she dies, he shall be sentenced to 28000 denars, which make 700 shillings.
summary: A person who hits a pregnant free woman and causes her death must pay 28000 denars (700 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have killed a free woman after she has begun bearing children, he shall be sentenced to 24000 denars, which make 600 shillings.
summary: A person who kills a free woman after she has begun bearing children must pay 24000 denars (600 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: After she can have no more children, he who kills her shall be sentenced to 8000 denars, which make 200, shillings.
summary: A person who kills a free woman after she can have no more children must pay 8000 denars (200 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one, man or woman, shall have called a woman harlot, and shall not have been able to prove it, he shall be sentenced to 1800 denars, which make 45 shillings.
summary: A person who calls a woman a harlot without proof must pay 1800 denars (45 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any person shall have called another "fox," he shall be sentenced to 3 shillings.
summary: A person who calls another a fox without proof must pay 3 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man shall have called another "hare," he shall be sentenced to 3 shillings.
summary: A man who calls another a hare without proof must pay 3 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man shall have brought it up against another that he have thrown away his shield, and shall not have been able to prove it, he shall be sentenced to 120 denars, which make 3 shillings.
summary: A man who accuses another of throwing away his shield without proof must pay 120 denars (3 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man shall have called another "spy" or "perjurer," and shall not have been able to prove it, he shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings.
summary: A man who calls another a spy or perjurer without proof must pay 600 denars (15 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have stolen a tame marked stag (-hound ?), trained to hunting, and it shall have been proved through witnesses that his master had him for hunting, or had killed with him two or three beasts, he shall be sentenced to 1800 denars, which make 45 shillings.
summary: Stealing a tame marked stag used for hunting results in a fine of 1800 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man shall have cut 3 staves by which a fence is bound or held together, or have stolen or cut the heads of 3 stakes, he shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings.
summary: Cutting or stealing three fence staves results in a fine of 600 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one shall have drawn a harrow through another's harvest after it has sprouted, or shall have gone through it with a waggon where there was no road, he shall be sentenced to 120 denars, which make 3 shillings.
summary: Drawing a harrow through another's harvest or driving a wagon through it without a road results in a fine of 120 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one shall have gone, where there is no way or path, through another's harvest which has already become thick, he shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings.
summary: Going through another's harvest where no path exists results in a fine of 600 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one shall have killed a free Frank, or a barbarian living under the Salic law, and it have been proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 8000 denars.
summary: Killing a free Frank or barbarian under Salic law results in a fine of 8000 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he shall have thrown him into a well or into the water, or shall have covered him with branches or anything else, to conceal him, he shall be sentenced to 24000 denars, which make 600 shillings.
summary: Throwing a man into a well or water and covering him to conceal the act results in a fine of 24000 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if any one has slain a man who is in the service of the king, he shall be sentenced to 24000 denars, which make 600 shillings.
summary: Slaying a man in the service of the king results in a fine of 24000 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he have put him in the water or in a well, and covered him with anything to conceal him, he shall be sentenced to 72000 denars, which make 1800 shillings.
summary: Throwing a man into a well or water and covering him to conceal the act results in a fine of 72000 denars.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have slain a Roman who eats in the king's palace, and it have been proved on him, he shall be sentenced to 12000 denars, which make 300 shillings.
summary: Killing a Roman who eats in the king's palace results in a fine of 12000 denars (300 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if the Roman shah not have been a landed proprietor and table companion of the king, he who killed him shall be sentenced to 4000 denars, which make 100 shillings.
summary: Killing a Roman who is not a landed proprietor and table companion of the king results in a fine of 4000 denars (100 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he shall have killed a Roman who was obliged to pay tribute, he shall be sentenced to shillings.
summary: Killing a Roman obliged to pay tribute results in a fine of shillings (amount unspecified).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have thrown a free man into a well, and he have escaped alive, he (the criminal) shall be sentenced to 4000 denars, which make 100 shillings.
summary: Throwing a free man into a well from which he escapes alive results in a fine of 4000 denars (100 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one wish to migrate to another village and if one or more who live in that village do not wish to receive him,-if there be only one who objects, he shall not have leave to move there.
summary: If a person wishes to migrate to another village and one or more residents object, the person is denied permission to move there if only one objector exists.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he shall have presumed to settle in that village in spite of his rejection by one or two men, then some one shall give him warning. And if he be unwilling to go away, he who gives him warning shall give him warning, with witnesses, as follows: I warn thee that thou mayst remain here this next night as the Salic law demands, and I warn thee that within 10 nights thou shalt go forth from this village. After another 10 nights he shall again come to him and warn him again within 10 nights to go away. If he still refuse to go, again 10 nights shall be added to the command, that the number of 30 nights may be full. If he will not go away even then, then he shall summon him to the "Thing," and present his witnesses as to the separate commands to leave. If he who has been warned will not then move away, and no valid reason detains him, and all the above warnings which we have mentioned have been given according to law: then he who gave him warning shall take the mutter into his own hands and request the "comes" to go to that place and expel him. And because he would not listen to the law, that man shall relinquish all that he has earned there, and, besides, shall be sentenced to 1200 denars, which make 30 shillings.
summary: If a person moves to a village despite rejection by one or two residents, repeated warnings are issued; if the person refuses to leave after 30 nights, they are expelled, lose all earnings, and are fined 1200 denars (30 shillings).

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if anyone have moved there, and within 12 months no one have given him warning, he shall remain as secure as the other neighbours.
summary: If a person moves to a village and no warning is given within 12 months, they are allowed to remain as a secure neighbor.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: The observance shall be that the Thunginus or Centenarius shall call together a "Thing," and shall have his shield in the "Thing," and shall demand three men as witnesses for each of the three transactions. He (the owner of the land to be transferred) shall seek a man who has no connection with himself, and shall throw a stalk into his lap. And to him into whose lap he has thrown the stalk he shall tell, concerning his property, how much of it-or whether the whole or a half-he wishes to give. He in whose lap he threw the stalk shall remain in his (the owner's) house, and shall collect three or more guests, and shall have the property-as much as is given him-in his power. And, afterwards, he to whom that property is entrusted shall discuss all these things with the witnesses collected afterwards, either before the king or in the regular "Thing," he shall give the property up to him for whom it was intended. He shall take the stalk in the "Thing," and, before 12 months are over, shall throw it into the lap of him whom the owner has named heir; and he shall restore not more nor less, but exactly as much as was entrusted to him.
summary: The transfer of land property involves a ritual with a stalk and witnesses; the property is entrusted to a neutral party who must return it exactly as given within 12 months.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: And if any one shall wish to say anything against this, three sworn witnesses shall say that they were in the "Thing " which the "Thunginus" or "Centenarius" called together, and that they saw that man who wished to give his property throw a stalk into the lap of him whom he had selected. They shall name by name him who threw his property into the lap of the other, and, likewise, shall name him whom he named his heir. And three other sworn witnesses shall say that he in whose lap the stalk was thrown had remained in the house of him who gave his property, and had there collected three or more guests and that they had eaten porridge at table, and that he had collected those who were bearing witness, and that those guests had thanked him for their entertainment. All this those other sworn witnesses shall say, and that he who received that property in his lap in the " Thing " held before the king, or in the regular public " Thing," did publicly, before the people, either in the presence of the king or in public " Thing "-namely on the Mallberg, before the "Thunginus"-throw the stalk into the lap of him whom the owner had named as heir. And thus 9 witnesses shall confirm all this.
summary: The law requires nine sworn witnesses to confirm that a person who wishes to give property to an heir publicly threw a stalk into the heir’s lap in a Thing assembly, and that the heir accepted it and hosted guests.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any freeman or feet have made to another a promise to pay, then he to whom the promise was made shall, within 40 days or within such term as was agreed when he made the promise, go to the house of that man with witnesses, or with appraisers. And if he (the debtor) be unwilling to make the promised payment, he shall be sentenced to 15 shillings above the debt which he had promised.
summary: If a freeman promises to pay another, the debtor must appear before the creditor’s house with witnesses within 40 days or the agreed term, or else be fined 15 shillings above the debt.
punishment: Fine of 15 shillings above the debt

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If he then be unwilling to pay, he (the creditor) shall summon him before the "Thing"; and thus accuse him: "I ask thee, 'Thunginus,' to bann my opponent who made me a promise to pay and owes me a debt." And he shall state how much he owes and promised to pay. Then the "Thunginus" shall say: " I bann thy opponent to what the Salic law decrees." Then he to whom the promise was made shall warn him (the debtor) to make no payment or pledge of payment to any body else until he have fulfilled his promise to him (the creditor). And straightway on that same day before the sun sets, he shall go to the house of that man with witnesses, and shall ask if he will pay that debt. If he will not, he (the creditor) shall wait until after sunset; then, if he have waited until after sunset, 120 denars, which make 3 shillings shall be added on to the debt. And this shall be done up to 3 times in 3 weeks. And if at the third time he will not pay all this, it (the sum) shall increase to 360 denars, or 9 shillings: so, namely, that, after each admonition or waiting until after sunset, 3 shillings shall be added to the debt.
summary: If the debtor fails to pay, the creditor may summon him before the Thing, and the debtor may be fined an additional 3 shillings each time, up to 9 shillings after three admonitions.
punishment: Fine of 3 shillings added each time, up to 9 shillings

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one be unwilling to fulfil his promise in the regular assembly,-then he to whom the promise was made shall go the count of that place, in whose district he lives, and shall take the stalk and shall say: oh count, that man made me a promise to pay, and I have lawfully summoned him before the court according to the Salic law on this matter; I pledge thee myself and my fortune that thou may'st safely seize his property. And he shall state the case to him, and shall tell how much he (the debtor) had agreed to pay. Then the count shall collect suitable bailiffs, and shall go with them to the house of him who made the promise and shall say: thou who art here present pay voluntarily to that man what thou didst promise, and choose any two of those bailiffs who shall appraise that from which thou shalt pay; and make good what thou cost owe, according to a just appraisal. But if ho will not hear, or be absent, then the bailiffs shall take from his property the value of the debt which he owes. And, according to the law, the accuser shall take two thirds of that which the debtor owes, and the count shall collect for himself the other third as peace money; unless the peace money shall have been paid to him before in this same matter.
summary: If a debtor refuses to pay, the creditor may petition the count to seize the debtor’s property, with the creditor receiving two‑thirds of the debt and the count one‑third as peace money.
punishment: Seizure of property; creditor receives two‑thirds, count one‑third

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If the count have been appealed to, and no sufficient reason, and no duty of the king, have detained him-and if he have put off going, and have sent no substitute to demand law and justice: he shall answer for it with his life, or shall redeem himself with his "wergeld."
summary: If a count fails to appear for a summons or delays justice, he may be held accountable with his life or must pay wergeld.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one slay a count, he shall be sentenced to 2400 debars, which make 600 shillings.
summary: If a person slays a count, he is sentenced to 2400 debars, which equal 600 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one shall have dug up and plundered a corpse already buried, and it shall have been proved on him, he shall be outlawed until the day when he comes to an agreement with the relatives of the dead man, and they ask for him that he be allowed to come among men. And whoever, before he come to an arrangement with the relative, shall give him bread or shelter-even if they are his relations or his own wife-shall be sentenced to 600 denars which make xv shillings.
summary: If a person digs up and plunders a buried corpse, he is outlawed until he reaches an agreement with the dead man’s relatives; anyone who gives him bread or shelter before that is fined 600 denars (15 shillings).
punishment: Outlawry until agreement; fine of 15 shillings for those who give aid

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But he who is proved to have committed the crime shall be sentenced to 8000 denars, which make 200 shillings.
summary: If a person is proven to have committed the crime of plundering a buried corpse, he is sentenced to 8000 denars, which equal 200 shillings.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man shall have scorned to come to court, and shall have put off fulfilling the injunction of the bailiffs, and shall not have been willing to consent to undergo the fine, or the kettle ordeal, or anything prescribed by law: then he (the plaintiff) shall summon him to the presence of the king. And there shall be 12 witnesses who-3 at n time being sworn-shall testify that they were present when the bailiff enjoined him (the accused) either to go to the kettle ordeal, or to agree concerning the fine; and that he had scorned the injunction. Then 3 others shall swear that they were there on the day when the bailiffs enjoined that he should free himself by the kettle ordeal or by composition; and that 40 days after that, in the "mallberg," he (the accuser) had again waited until after sunset, and that he (the accused) would not obey the law. Then he (the accuser) shall summon him before the king for a fortnight thence; and three witnesses shall swear that they were there when he summoned him and when he waited for sunset. If he does not then come, those 9, being sworn, shall give testimony as we have above explained. On that day likewise, if he do not come, he (the accuser) shall let the sun go down on him, and shall have 3 witnesses who shall be there when he waits till sunset. But if the accuser shall have fulfilled all this, and the accused shall not have been willing to come to any court, then the king, before whom he has been summoned, shall withdraw his protection from him. Then he shall be guilty, and all his goods shall belong to the fisc, or to him to whom the fisc may wish to give them. And whoever shall have fed or housed him-even if it were his own wife-shall be sentenced to 600 denars, which make 15 shillings; until he (the debtor) shall have made good all that has been laid to his charge.
summary: A man who refuses to attend court or comply with bailiff orders is summoned to the king; if he still refuses, his property is seized and anyone who feeds or houses him is fined 600 denars.
punishment: Seizure of property; 600 denars fine for host

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one have killed a man, and, having given up all his property, has not enough to comply with the full terms of the law, he shall present 12 sworn witnesses to the effect that, neither above the earth nor under it, has he any more property than he has already given. And he shall afterwards go into his house, and shall collect in his hand dust from the four corners of it, and shall afterwards stand upon the threshold, looking inwards into the house. And then, with his left hand, he shall throw over his shoulder some of that dust on the nearest relative that he has. But if his father and (his father's) brothers have already paid, he shall then throw that dust on their (the brothers') children-that is, over three (relatives) who are nearest on the father's and three on the mother's side. And after that, in his shirt, without girdle and without shoes, a staff in his hand, he shall spring over the hedge. And then those three shall pay half of what is lacking of the compounding money or the legal fine; that is, those others who are descended in the paternal line shall do this.
summary: A murderer who cannot pay the full fine must present witnesses, perform a symbolic dust‑throwing ritual, and his relatives must contribute half the remaining fine.
punishment: Relatives pay half of remaining fine

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if there be one of those relatives who has not enough to pay his whole indebtedness, he, the poorer one, shall in turn throw the "chrenecruda" on him of them who has the most, so that he shall pay the whole fine.
summary: If a relative cannot pay the full fine, the wealthiest relative must cover the shortfall.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if he also have not enough to pay the whole then he who has charge of the murderer shall bring him before the " Thing," and afterwards to 4 Things in order that they (his friends) may take him under their protection. And if no one have taken him under his protection -that is, so as to redeem him for what he can not pay- then he shall have to atone with his life.
summary: If no relative can pay the fine, the murderer is brought before the Thing and, if unprotected, must atone with his life.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any man die and leave no sons, if the father and mother survive, they shall inherit.
summary: If a man dies without sons, his surviving parents inherit his estate.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If the father and mother do not survive, and he leave brothers or sisters, they shall inherit.
summary: If a man dies without parents, his brothers or sisters inherit his estate.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if there are none, the sisters of the father shall inherit.
summary: If a man dies without parents or siblings, the sisters of his father inherit his estate.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if there are no sisters of tile father, the sisters of the mother shall claim that inheritance.
summary: If a man dies without parents, siblings, or paternal sisters, the sisters of his mother inherit his estate.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If there are none of these, the nearest relatives on the father's side shall succeed to that inheritance.
summary: If no eligible heirs exist, the nearest paternal relatives inherit the property.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But of Salic land no portion of the inheritance shall come to a woman: but the whole inheritance of the land shall come to the male sex.
summary: Women cannot inherit Salic land; all inheritance goes to males.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: If any one's father have been killed, the sons shall have half the compounding money (wergeld); and the other half the nearest relatives, as well on the mother's as on the father's side, shall divide among themselves.
summary: If a father is killed, sons receive half the wergeld and the other half is divided among nearest relatives on both sides.

source: The Salic Law, trans. E. F. Henderson (1896)
text: But if there are no relatives, paternal or maternal that portion shall go to the fisc.
summary: If no relatives exist, the remaining portion of the wergeld goes to the state treasury.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: A winner at the Olympic Games is paid five hundred drachmas from the treasury, and a winner at the Isthmian Games a hundred.
summary: Olympic winners receive five hundred drachmas and Isthmian winners receive one hundred drachmas from the treasury.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: The laws are to stand for a hundred years, written on revolving wooden axles that anyone can turn and read.
summary: Laws are written on revolving wooden axles that anyone can turn and read for a hundred years.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: A foreigner may become a citizen only if he is exiled from his own country for good, or moves to Athens with his whole household to practise a trade.
summary: A foreigner may become an Athenian citizen only if he is exiled from his homeland or moves to Athens with his household to practice a trade.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: The council of the Areopagus must examine how every man makes his living, and punish anyone who lives in idleness.
summary: The Areopagus must examine every man's livelihood and punish anyone who lives in idleness.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Mourners may not tear their flesh, recite set laments or wail at another family's funeral; no ox may be sacrificed at the grave, and no more than three garments may be buried with the dead.
summary: Mourners may not tear flesh, recite laments, wail at another family's funeral, sacrifice an ox at a grave, or bury more than three garments with the dead.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: A citizen who takes neither side when the city is torn by civil strife loses his rights as a citizen.
summary: A citizen who takes no side during civil strife loses his rights as a citizen.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Of all the produce of Attica, only olive oil may be sold abroad. The archon must curse anyone who exports anything else, or pay a hundred drachmas himself.
summary: Only olive oil may be sold abroad; anyone exporting other goods must be cursed by the archon or pay 100 drachmas himself.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Plant trees at least five feet from your neighbour's land, and fig or olive trees nine feet; dig a ditch as far from his land as it is deep; keep beehives three hundred feet from his.
summary: Plant trees at specified distances from neighbors' land, dig ditches and keep beehives at required distances.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: No one may speak ill of the dead. Abusing the living in a temple, a court, a public office or at a festival costs five drachmas: three to the person insulted and two to the treasury.
summary: No one may speak ill of the dead; abusing the living in a temple, court, public office or festival costs 5 drachmas (3 to the insulted person, 2 to the treasury).

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Where a public well is within four furlongs, you must use it; farther away, dig your own. If you dig ten fathoms and find no water, you may take a six-gallon pitcher from your neighbour's well twice a day.
summary: Use a public well within four furlongs; otherwise dig your own well, and if you find none you may take a six-gallon pitcher from a neighbor twice a day.

source: Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 20-24, trans. B. Perrin (1914) (paraphrased)
text: Anyone who kills a wolf earns five drachmas from the treasury, and one drachma for a wolf cub.
summary: Anyone who kills a wolf earns 5 drachmas from the treasury, and one drachma for a wolf cub.

source: Disney, Aladdin (paraphrased)
text: A genie may not kill anyone and may not bring anyone back from the dead.
summary: A genie may not kill anyone and may not bring anyone back from the dead.

source: Disney, Aladdin (paraphrased)
text: Whoever rubs the lamp gets three wishes from the genie, and may not wish for more wishes.
summary: Whoever rubs the lamp gets three wishes from the genie, and may not wish for more wishes.

source: George Orwell, Animal Farm (paraphrased)
text: No animal may drink alcohol; once the pigs discover whisky, the commandment turns out to have said not to excess.
summary: No animal may drink alcohol; once the pigs discover whisky, the commandment turns out to have said not to excess.

source: George Orwell, Animal Farm (paraphrased)
text: No animal may sleep in a bed; once the pigs move into the farmhouse, the commandment turns out to have said no bed with sheets.
summary: No animal may sleep in a bed; once the pigs move into the farmhouse, the commandment turns out to have said no bed with sheets.

source: George Orwell, Animal Farm (paraphrased)
text: All animals are equal; by the end, some animals are more equal than others.
summary: All animals are equal; by the end, some animals are more equal than others.

source: Isaac Asimov, the robot stories (paraphrased)
text: A robot may not harm a human being, or let one come to harm through inaction; it must obey human orders unless that would harm a human; and it must protect itself unless that conflicts with the first two laws.
summary: A robot may not harm a human being, or let one come to harm through inaction; it must obey human orders unless that would harm a human; and it must protect itself unless that conflicts with the first two laws.

source: Isaac Asimov, the robot stories (paraphrased)
text: Above all three laws stands the Zeroth: a robot may not harm humanity as a whole, or let it come to harm through inaction.
summary: Above all three laws stands the Zeroth: a robot may not harm humanity as a whole, or let it come to harm through inaction.

source: Avatar: The Last Airbender (paraphrased)
text: In the Fire Nation, a question of honour may be settled by an Agni Kai, a duel of firebending.
summary: In the Fire Nation, a question of honour may be settled by an Agni Kai, a duel of firebending.

source: Avatar: The Last Airbender (paraphrased)
text: In Ba Sing Se, no one may mention the war, and the secret police make sure of it.
summary: No one may mention the war, and the secret police enforce this.

source: Back to the Future (paraphrased)
citation: Back to the Future Part II (1989)
text: A time traveller must avoid meeting his own past or future self, in case it tears the space-time continuum apart.
summary: A time traveller must avoid meeting his own past or future self to prevent tearing the space-time continuum.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part II (paraphrased)
text: No law may contain more words than there are letters in the alphabet, which has twenty-two, and writing a commentary on any law is a capital crime.
summary: No law may contain more words than there are letters in the alphabet (22), and writing a commentary on any law is a capital crime.

source: Joseph Heller, Catch-22 (paraphrased)
text: A pilot who is crazy may be grounded, but only if he asks, and asking to be grounded from deadly missions proves he is sane, so he must fly.
summary: A pilot who is crazy may be grounded only if he asks, but asking to be grounded proves he is sane, so he must fly.

source: Terry Pratchett, the Discworld novels (paraphrased)
text: Ankh-Morpork has the form of democracy called One Man, One Vote: the Patrician is the man, and he has the vote.
summary: Ankh-Morpork has a democracy called One Man, One Vote where the Patrician is the sole voter.

source: Terry Pratchett, the Discworld novels (paraphrased)
citation: The Discworld novels, from Guards! Guards! (1989)
text: Theft in Ankh-Morpork is licensed: the Thieves' Guild may commit an agreed amount of crime each year, gives its victims a receipt, and deals harshly with unlicensed thieves. Citizens can pay the Guild a yearly fee to be left alone.
summary: Theft in Ankh-Morpork is licensed; the Thieves' Guild may commit an agreed amount of crime each year, gives victims a receipt, and deals harshly with unlicensed thieves; citizens can pay a yearly fee to be left alone.

source: Doctor Who (paraphrased)
citation: Doctor Who, The Waters of Mars (2009)
text: Some moments are fixed points in time, and a Time Lord must never change them, however much he wants to.
summary: A Time Lord must never change fixed points in time, however much he wants to.

source: Doctor Who (paraphrased)
text: The First Law of Time forbids a Time Lord from meeting earlier versions of himself.
summary: The First Law of Time forbids a Time Lord from meeting earlier versions of himself.

source: Frank Herbert, Dune (paraphrased)
text: Under the Great Convention, using atomic weapons against human beings is forbidden.
summary: Using atomic weapons against human beings is forbidden under the Great Convention.

source: Frank Herbert, Dune (paraphrased)
text: A Fremen leader can be challenged to single combat, and the winner leads the tribe.
summary: A Fremen leader may be challenged to single combat, and the victor becomes the tribe's leader.

source: Frank Herbert, Dune (paraphrased)
text: Since the Butlerian Jihad, no one may build a machine in the likeness of a human mind.
summary: No one may build a machine resembling a human mind since the Butlerian Jihad.

source: Frank Herbert, Dune (paraphrased)
text: Among the Fremen, the water of the dead belongs to the tribe, and to spit before someone is a gift of honour.
summary: The water of the dead belongs to the Fremen tribe, and spitting before someone is considered a gift of honour.

source: Samuel Butler, Erewhon (1872) (paraphrased)
citation: Erewhon, chapters 23-25 (The Book of the Machines)
text: Every machine was destroyed centuries ago, and keeping one is a serious offence, for fear that machines will evolve and take over.
summary: Keeping a machine is a serious offence because machines may evolve and take over.

source: Samuel Butler, Erewhon (1872) (paraphrased)
text: Misfortune is a crime: losing your money or your health is punished, while wrongdoing is treated as an illness.
summary: Misfortune, such as losing money or health, is a crime punishable, while wrongdoing is treated as an illness.

source: Ray Bradbury, Fahrenheit 451 (paraphrased)
text: Owning books is a crime, and firemen no longer put out fires: they come to burn the books.
summary: Owning books is a crime, and firemen are tasked with burning them instead of putting out fires.

source: Fairy tales by Charles Perrault (1697), Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont (1756) and Robert Southey (1837) (paraphrased)
citation: Hans Christian Andersen, The Emperor's New Clothes (1837)
text: Cloth woven by the two swindlers is said to be invisible to anyone unfit for his office or hopelessly stupid, so no one dares admit he cannot see it, not even the emperor.
summary: Cloth woven by two swindlers is invisible to those unfit for office or hopelessly stupid, and no one may admit they cannot see it, not even the emperor.

source: Fairy tales by Charles Perrault (1697), Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont (1756) and Robert Southey (1837) (paraphrased)
text: A ball gown granted by a fairy godmother lasts only until midnight; stay later and you are back in rags.
summary: A ball gown granted by a fairy godmother lasts only until midnight; staying later returns the wearer to rags.

source: Fairy tales by Charles Perrault (1697), Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont (1756) and Robert Southey (1837) (paraphrased)
citation: Robert Southey, The Story of the Three Bears (1837)
text: Whoever walks into the bears' house uninvited, eats their porridge and breaks a chair must answer to the bears when they come home.
summary: Anyone who walks into the bears' house uninvited, eats their porridge, and breaks a chair must answer to the bears when they return.

source: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine (paraphrased)
citation: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition
text: Rule 1: once you have their money, never give it back.
summary: Once you have someone's money, you must never give it back.

source: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine (paraphrased)
citation: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition
text: Rule 285: no good deed ever goes unpunished.
summary: No good deed ever goes unpunished.

source: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine (paraphrased)
citation: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition
text: Rule 3: never pay more for an acquisition than you have to.
summary: Never pay more for an acquisition than you have to.

source: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine (paraphrased)
citation: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition
text: Rules 34 and 35: war is good for business, and so is peace.
summary: War is good for business, and so is peace.

source: Fight Club (paraphrased)
text: The first rule of the club, and the second, is that members never talk about it.
summary: Members must not discuss the club.

source: Pixar, Finding Nemo (paraphrased)
text: Members of the sharks' support group pledge that fish are friends, not food.
summary: Shark support group members pledge fish are friends, not food.

source: Isaac Asimov, Foundation (paraphrased)
text: When Hari Seldon predicted the fall of the Empire, the Commission of Public Safety tried him and exiled him and his scientists to Terminus, a planet at the edge of the galaxy, to write the Encyclopedia Galactica.
summary: Hari Seldon and his scientists are tried and exiled to Terminus.

source: Isaac Asimov, Foundation (paraphrased)
text: On Terminus, violence is the last refuge of the incompetent: a crisis is solved by wit, never by force.
summary: Crisis on Terminus is solved by wit, not force.

source: Isaac Asimov, Foundation (paraphrased)
text: The neighbouring kingdoms get nuclear power only through priests trained on Terminus, who tend it as a sacred mystery.
summary: Nuclear power is provided by priests trained on Terminus.

source: Isaac Asimov, Foundation (paraphrased)
text: At every crisis Seldon foresaw, the Time Vault on Terminus opens and his recorded image explains what has just happened.
summary: The Time Vault opens at crises and Seldon’s recorded image explains events.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
citation: A Game of Thrones, chapter 1 (Bran); Game of Thrones, season 1, episode 1
text: A sworn brother of the Night's Watch who deserts his post is put to death, and Lord Eddard Stark carries out the sentence himself.
summary: A sworn brother of the Night's Watch who deserts his post is put to death, and Lord Eddard Stark carries out the sentence.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)

text: Once a guest has eaten a host's bread and salt, neither may harm the other under that roof, and breaking guest right is among the worst crimes in Westeros.
summary: Once a guest has eaten a host's bread and salt, neither may harm the other under that roof, and breaking guest right is among the worst crimes in Westeros.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
text: Among the Ironborn, anything worth having is paid for with the iron price, taken by force rather than bought with gold, and buying what you could have taken is shameful.
summary: Among the Ironborn, anything worth having is paid for with the iron price, taken by force rather than bought with gold, and buying what you could have taken is shameful.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
text: Knights of the Kingsguard serve for life and may hold no lands of their own.
summary: Knights of the Kingsguard must serve for life and cannot own lands.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
