text: A brother of the Night's Watch serves for life, holds no lands and wears no crown.
summary: A brother of the Night's Watch must serve for life, cannot own lands, and cannot wear a crown.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
citation: A Game of Thrones; Game of Thrones, season 1
text: In the North, the lord who passes a sentence of death must carry it out himself.
summary: A lord who passes a death sentence in the North must carry it out himself.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
citation: A Game of Thrones; Game of Thrones, season 1
text: A convicted criminal may take the black instead of his sentence: he joins the Night's Watch and serves at the Wall for life.
summary: A convicted criminal may take the black instead of his sentence, joining the Night's Watch for life.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
citation: A Game of Thrones; House of the Dragon, season 1
text: The Hand of the King speaks with the king's voice and rules in his name when the king is absent or unwell.
summary: The Hand of the King speaks with the king's voice and rules in his name when the king is absent or unwell.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
citation: A Game of Thrones; Game of Thrones, season 1
text: An accused may demand a trial by combat, so that the gods decide his guilt, and may fight himself or name a champion.
summary: An accused may demand a trial by combat, allowing the accused or a champion to fight to determine guilt.

source: George R. R. Martin, A Game of Thrones (paraphrased)
text: No blade may be drawn and no blood shed in the sacred city of Vaes Dothrak.
summary: No blade may be drawn and no blood shed in the sacred city of Vaes Dothrak.

source: Ghostbusters (paraphrased)
text: Never cross the proton streams: it would be very, very bad.
summary: Never cross the proton streams.

source: Gremlins (paraphrased)
text: Keep a mogwai out of bright light, never let it get wet, and never, ever feed it after midnight.
summary: Keep a mogwai out of bright light, dry, and never feed after midnight.

source: J. K. Rowling, the Harry Potter novels (paraphrased)
citation: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
text: Nobody may apparate without passing the Ministry's test, and splinching yourself is the usual way to fail it.
summary: The law forbids anyone from apparating without passing the Ministry's test, and failing it by splinching is the usual way to fail.

source: J. K. Rowling, the Harry Potter novels (paraphrased)
citation: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
text: Serious crimes earn a sentence in Azkaban, the wizards' prison on an island in the North Sea, guarded by Dementors.
summary: Serious crimes earn a sentence in Azkaban, the wizards' prison guarded by Dementors.

source: J. K. Rowling, the Harry Potter novels (paraphrased)
citation: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, chapter 5
text: Robbing Gringotts is the height of folly: the goblins' vaults lie miles underground, behind enchantments and worse.
summary: The law forbids robbing Gringotts, the goblin bank.

source: J. K. Rowling, the Harry Potter novels (paraphrased)
citation: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, chapter 15
text: Students caught breaking school rules, such as roaming the castle at night, lose points for their house and are given detention.
summary: Students caught breaking school rules lose points for their house and are given detention.

source: J. K. Rowling, the Harry Potter novels (paraphrased)
text: Under the International Statute of Wizarding Secrecy, witches and wizards must hide magic from Muggles.
summary: The law requires witches and wizards to hide magic from Muggles.

source: J. K. Rowling, the Harry Potter novels (paraphrased)
citation: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, chapter 14
text: Using any of the three Unforgivable Curses on another person is enough to earn a life sentence in Azkaban, the wizards' prison.
summary: Using any of the three Unforgivable Curses on another person earns a life sentence in Azkaban.

jurisdiction_name: The Galaxy, as the Guide sees it
source: Douglas Adams, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (paraphrased)
citation: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (1979)
text: The plans to demolish Earth for a hyperspace bypass were on display at the planning office on Alpha Centauri for fifty years, so it is far too late to object.
summary: The law states that plans to demolish Earth for a hyperspace bypass were on display for fifty years, so it is too late to object.

source: DreamWorks, How to Train Your Dragon (paraphrased)
text: On Berk, every Viking must fight dragons, and befriending one is unthinkable.
summary: The law requires every Viking on Berk to fight dragons, and befriending one is unthinkable.

source: Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games trilogy (paraphrased)
text: Watching the Games on television is mandatory for every citizen of Panem.
summary: All citizens must watch the Games on television.

source: Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games trilogy (paraphrased)
text: Leaving District 12 through the fence to hunt in the woods is forbidden, though Katniss does it anyway and sells game to the Peacekeepers, who look the other way.
summary: Leaving District 12 to hunt in the woods is forbidden, but Katniss does it and sells game to Peacekeepers who ignore it.

source: Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games trilogy (paraphrased)
text: Every twenty-fifth year, a Quarter Quell adds a twist to the Games: for the 75th, the tributes were reaped from the living victors.
summary: Every twenty-fifth year a Quarter Quell adds a twist to the Games; for the 75th, tributes were reaped from living victors.

source: Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games trilogy (paraphrased)
text: Citizens may not travel between districts without the Capitol's permission.
summary: Citizens may not travel between districts without the Capitol's permission.

source: Suzanne Collins, The Hunger Games trilogy (paraphrased)
text: A victor of the Games gets a house in the Victors' Village and enough to live on for life, and their district gets extra food for a year.
summary: A victor receives a house in the Victors' Village and lifetime sustenance, and their district gets extra food for a year.

source: Pixar, The Incredibles (paraphrased)
text: A superhero costume must never have a cape: they snag on everything.
summary: The law forbids superhero costumes from having a cape.

source: Pixar, The Incredibles (paraphrased)
text: After a wave of lawsuits, superheroes are banned from heroics and must live quiet lives under the government's relocation programme.
summary: The law bans superheroes from heroics and requires them to live quiet lives under a relocation programme.

source: Rudyard Kipling, The Law of the Jungle, in The Second Jungle Book (1895) (paraphrased)
text: A cub may claim a share of any kill, and no one may refuse a hungry yearling his meal.
summary: A cub may claim a share of any kill, and no one may refuse a hungry yearling his meal.

source: Rudyard Kipling, The Law of the Jungle, in The Second Jungle Book (1895) (paraphrased)
text: A wolf's lair is his refuge: not even the Head Wolf or the Council may enter it.
summary: A wolf's lair is his refuge; not even the Head Wolf or the Council may enter it.

source: Rudyard Kipling, The Law of the Jungle, in The Second Jungle Book (1895) (paraphrased)
text: The kill of the pack is the meat of the pack: eat where it lies, and no one may carry it off.
summary: The kill of the pack is the meat of the pack: eat where it lies, and no one may carry it off.

source: Rudyard Kipling, The Law of the Jungle, in The Second Jungle Book (1895) (paraphrased)
text: When two packs meet on the trail, let them pass, and no wolf of a pack may fight another until the Council has heard the quarrel.
summary: No wolf may fight another until the Council has heard the quarrel.

source: Rudyard Kipling, The Law of the Jungle, in The Second Jungle Book (1895) (paraphrased)
text: Wash daily from nose to tail, drink deeply but never too deeply, and remember that night is for hunting and day for sleep.
summary: Animals must wash daily and observe hunting at night and sleep during the day.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
citation: Gulliver's Travels, part I, chapter 3, article 2
text: He may not enter the capital without an express order, and the inhabitants must have two hours' warning to stay indoors.
summary: A person may not enter the capital without an express order, and inhabitants must be warned two hours before staying indoors.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
text: By imperial edict, eggs must be broken at the smaller end, upon great penalties. The dispute has already caused six rebellions.
summary: Eggs must be broken at the smaller end, under great penalties.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
text: Whoever falsely accuses another person is put to death, and the innocent party is repaid four times over for the time, danger and trouble it cost them.
summary: A false accuser is put to death, and the innocent party is repaid four times over.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
text: Fraud is punished more harshly than theft, because honesty cannot protect itself against it.
summary: Fraud is punished more harshly than theft.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
text: Ingratitude is a capital crime.
summary: Ingratitude is a capital crime.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
citation: Gulliver's Travels, part I, chapter 3, article 1
text: The Man-Mountain may not leave the kingdom without a licence under the great seal.
summary: The Man-Mountain may not leave the kingdom without a licence under the great seal.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
text: In return, he receives a daily allowance of food and drink enough for 1,724 Lilliputians.
summary: The law provides a daily allowance of food and drink sufficient for 1,724 Lilliputians.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
citation: Gulliver's Travels, part I, chapter 3, article 3
text: He must keep to the main high roads, and not walk or lie down in meadows or cornfields.
summary: The law requires the subject to travel only on main high roads and prohibits walking or lying down in meadows or cornfields.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
citation: Gulliver's Travels, part I, chapter 3, article 7
text: He must help the workmen lift the great stones for the royal buildings and the park wall.
summary: The law obligates the subject to assist workmen in lifting large stones for royal buildings and a park wall.

source: Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726), part I (paraphrased)
citation: Gulliver's Travels, part I, chapter 3, article 4
text: He must take the utmost care not to trample any subject, horse or carriage, and may not pick up any subject without their consent.
summary: The law forbids trampling any subject, horse, or carriage and prohibits picking up any subject without their consent.

source: Disney, The Lion King (paraphrased)
text: Everything the light touches belongs to the Pride Lands, and no lion may go to the shadowy place beyond the borders.
summary: The law states that everything the light touches belongs to the Pride Lands, and no lion may go beyond the borders into the shadowy place.

source: Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass (1871) (paraphrased)
text: The rule is jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today.
summary: The law states that jam is allowed tomorrow and yesterday, but not today.

source: Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass (1871) (paraphrased)
text: Here it takes all the running you can do to stay in the same place; to get anywhere else, you must run twice as fast.
summary: The law requires that to stay in the same place you must run, and to move elsewhere you must run twice as fast.

source: Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass (1871) (paraphrased)
text: There are three hundred and sixty-four days a year for un-birthday presents, and only one for birthday presents.
summary: The law declares 364 days a year for un-birthday presents and only one day for birthday presents.

source: Men in Black (paraphrased)
text: No ordinary person may know that aliens live on Earth: any witness has the memory erased with a flash of the neuralyzer.
summary: Ordinary people may not know aliens live on Earth; witnesses have their memory erased by a neuralyzer.

source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (paraphrased)
citation: The Fellowship of the Ring (1954), prologue
text: On a hobbit's birthday, the hobbit gives presents to everyone else.
summary: A hobbit must give presents to everyone else on their birthday.

source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (paraphrased)
text: The West-gate of Moria opens for anyone who says the Elvish word for friend.
summary: The West-gate of Moria opens for anyone who says the Elvish word for friend.

source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (paraphrased)
text: The riddle game is sacred and very ancient: even wicked creatures fear to cheat at it.
summary: Cheating at the sacred riddle game is forbidden; even wicked creatures fear to cheat.

source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (paraphrased)
citation: The Fellowship of the Ring (1954), prologue
text: The Shire has hardly any government: hobbits obey the Rules, ancient and just, of their own free will.
summary: Hobbits must obey the Rules of their own free will in the Shire.

source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (paraphrased)
text: In Gondor, the Steward rules in the king's name until the king returns, however many centuries that takes.
summary: In Gondor, the Steward rules in the king's name until the king returns, however many centuries that takes.

source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (paraphrased)
text: No stranger may enter the hall of Meduseld armed: every weapon, even a wizard's staff, must be left at the door.
summary: No stranger may enter the hall of Meduseld armed; every weapon must be left at the door.

source: W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, The Mikado (1885) (paraphrased)
text: The Lord High Executioner is himself under sentence of death, so he cannot execute anyone else until he has executed himself.
summary: The law states that the Lord High Executioner is under a death sentence and cannot execute anyone until he has executed himself.

source: W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, The Mikado (1885) (paraphrased)
text: Every punishment must fit the crime: a billiard sharp, for example, must play forever on a cloth untrue, with a twisted cue and elliptical billiard balls.
summary: The law requires punishments to match the crime, such as a billiard cue playing forever on a false cloth with twisted cue and elliptical balls.

source: Disney, Moana (paraphrased)
text: On Motunui, no one sails beyond the reef.
summary: No one may sail beyond the reef on Motunui.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
citation: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), chapter 13
text: By the Deep Magic from the Dawn of Time, every traitor belongs to the White Witch, and she has a right to his life.
summary: A traitor is owned by the White Witch and may be killed by her.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
citation: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), chapter 15
text: By a deeper magic still, if a willing victim who has done no treachery dies in a traitor's place, the Stone Table cracks and death itself works backwards.
summary: If a willing non‑treacherous victim dies in a traitor’s place, the Stone Table cracks and death reverses.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
citation: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), chapter 6
text: Comforting the Witch's enemies, harbouring spies or befriending humans is high treason, and the Witch turns traitors to stone.
summary: Harbouring spies or befriending humans is treason; the Witch turns traitors to stone.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
citation: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), chapter 2
text: Under the White Witch it is always winter in Narnia, and never Christmas.
summary: Under the White Witch, it is always winter and never Christmas in Narnia.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
citation: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), chapter 17
text: Whoever is crowned king or queen in Narnia stays a king or queen of Narnia for life, even after going home.
summary: A crowned king or queen remains that title for life, even after leaving Narnia.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
text: A Talking Beast of Narnia may never be hunted or eaten; to eat one, even by mistake, is a horror.
summary: A Talking Beast may not be hunted or eaten; doing so is a horror.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
text: The fruit of the walled garden may be picked only for others; whoever climbs the wall or takes the fruit for himself gets what he wanted, and despair along with it.
summary: Fruit from the walled garden may only be taken for others; climbing the wall or taking fruit for oneself causes despair.

source: C. S. Lewis, The Chronicles of Narnia (paraphrased)
text: Aslan's signs must be remembered and obeyed: the lost prince will be the first person to ask you to do something in Aslan's name.
summary: Aslan’s signs must be remembered and obeyed; the lost prince will first ask you to act in Aslan’s name.

source: George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (paraphrased)
text: Thinking a forbidden thought is itself a crime, and the Thought Police hunt for it, even in the way a face moves.
summary: Thinking a forbidden thought is a crime and the Thought Police may hunt for it, even by observing facial movements.

source: L. Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900) (paraphrased)
citation: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, chapter 11
text: The Wizard sees visitors only one at a time, on a day he chooses, and grants a wish only in exchange for a service.
summary: The Wizard may see only one visitor at a time on a day he chooses and will grant a wish only if the visitor provides a service.

source: L. Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900) (paraphrased)
citation: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, chapter 10
text: Everyone in the Emerald City must wear green spectacles, locked on by the Guardian of the Gates, or the city's brightness would blind them.
summary: All residents of Emerald City must wear green spectacles locked on by the Guardian of the Gates or the city's brightness would blind them.

source: Norton Juster, The Phantom Tollbooth (paraphrased)
text: In the Doldrums, thinking and laughing are against the law; the day is filled with naps, daydreams and lingering.
summary: Thinking and laughing are illegal; the day is filled with naps, daydreams and lingering.

source: Carlo Collodi, The Adventures of Pinocchio (1883) (paraphrased)
text: In the town of Catchfools, the judge sends the victim of a robbery to prison, for being foolish enough to be robbed.
summary: A robbery victim is sent to prison for being foolish enough to be robbed.

source: W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, The Pirates of Penzance (1879) (paraphrased)
citation: The Pirates of Penzance, act II
text: An apprentice bound until his twenty-first birthday who was born on 29 February must serve until 1940, having had only five birthdays.
summary: An apprentice born on February 29 who is bound until his twenty‑first birthday must serve until 1940, having had only five birthdays.

source: W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, The Pirates of Penzance (1879) (paraphrased)
citation: The Pirates of Penzance, act I
text: The pirates never attack a weaker party and always let orphans go free, which is why every crew they capture claims to be orphans.
summary: Pirates are prohibited from attacking weaker parties and must release orphans, leading crews to claim orphan status.

jurisdiction_name: The Caribbean, under the Pirate Code
source: Pirates of the Caribbean (paraphrased)
citation: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl (2003)
text: The Pirate Code is more what you would call guidelines than actual rules.
summary: The Pirate Code is merely guidelines, not enforceable rules.

jurisdiction_name: The Caribbean, under the Pirate Code
source: Pirates of the Caribbean (paraphrased)
citation: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl (2003)
text: Under the Pirate Code, anyone who demands parley must be taken unharmed to the captain to negotiate.
summary: Anyone demanding parley must be taken unharmed to the captain for negotiation.

source: The Pokémon games (paraphrased)
text: Only a trainer who has won eight Gym badges may challenge the Pokémon League.
summary: Only a trainer who has won eight Gym badges may challenge the Pokémon League.

source: The Pokémon games (paraphrased)
text: A trainer who loses a battle hands over prize money to the winner.
summary: A trainer who loses a battle must hand over prize money to the winner.

source: Pierce Brown, Red Rising (paraphrased)
text: At the Institute, each house is a student army, and a house wins by capturing the standards of all the others.
summary: At the Institute, each house is a student army; a house wins by capturing all other houses' standards.

source: Pierce Brown, Red Rising (paraphrased)
text: Each quarter, the mining clan that digs the most helium-3 wins the Laurel: extra food and comforts for the clan.
summary: The mining clan that digs the most helium‑3 each quarter wins the Laurel, gaining extra food and comforts for the clan.

source: William Shakespeare's plays (paraphrased)
text: To end their quarrel without a duel, the king banishes Bolingbroke for ten years, soon cut to six, and Mowbray for life.
summary: The king banishes Bolingbroke for ten years, later reduced to six, and Mowbray for life.

source: William Shakespeare's plays (paraphrased)
text: For telling the king an unwelcome truth, the Earl of Kent is banished: he has five days to prepare, and on the sixth must leave the kingdom.
summary: The Earl of Kent is banished for telling the king an unwelcome truth, given five days to prepare and must leave on the sixth.

source: William Shakespeare's plays (paraphrased)
text: For killing Tybalt in a street brawl, Romeo is banished from Verona; if he is found there again, he dies.
summary: Killing Tybalt in a street brawl banishes Romeo from Verona; if he returns, he is executed.

source: Star Trek (paraphrased)
text: Under the Prime Directive, Starfleet may not interfere with the natural development of a less advanced civilisation.
summary: Starfleet may not interfere with the natural development of a less advanced civilisation under the Prime Directive.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
citation: Star Wars: Episode V, The Empire Strikes Back (1980)
text: A Jedi uses the Force for knowledge and defence, never to attack.
summary: A Jedi may use the Force for knowledge and defence, never to attack.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
text: A Mandalorian of the creed never removes the helmet in front of another living being.
summary: A Mandalorian of the creed must never remove the helmet in front of another living being.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
citation: Star Wars: Episode I, The Phantom Menace (1999)
text: Any senator may call a vote of no confidence in the Supreme Chancellor, and a new Chancellor is elected if it passes.
summary: Any senator may call a vote of no confidence in the Supreme Chancellor, and a new Chancellor is elected if it passes.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
citation: Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope (1977)
text: The Mos Eisley cantina does not serve droids; they wait outside.
summary: The Mos Eisley cantina does not serve droids; they must wait outside.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
citation: Star Wars: Episode I, The Phantom Menace (1999)
text: There are only ever two Sith at a time: a master and an apprentice.
summary: There are only ever two Sith at a time: a master and an apprentice.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
citation: Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope (1977)
text: The Emperor has dissolved the Imperial Senate, and the regional governors now rule their systems directly.
summary: The Emperor has dissolved the Imperial Senate, and the regional governors now rule their systems directly.

source: The Star Wars films and series (paraphrased)
citation: Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope (1977)
text: A smuggler who dumps a cargo to escape an inspection still owes the Hutt its full price.
summary: A smuggler who dumps cargo to avoid inspection still owes the Hutt the full price.

source: Pixar, Toy Story (paraphrased)
text: Toys must go limp and silent the moment a human might see them move.
summary: Toys must become limp and silent when a human might see them move.

source: Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island (1883) (paraphrased)
text: A pirate handed the black spot has been summoned by his crew, and must answer to them by the time it names.
summary: A pirate who receives the black spot must answer to his crew by the time it names him.

source: Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island (1883) (paraphrased)
text: A crew may maroon a man on a lonely island, as Ben Gunn's shipmates did; he lived there alone for three years, dreaming of toasted cheese.
summary: A crew may maroon a man on a lonely island; he may live there alone for years.

source: Pixar, WALL-E (paraphrased)
text: Directive A113: the starliner must never return to Earth.
summary: The starliner must never return to Earth.

source: Kenneth Grahame, The Wind in the Willows (1908) (paraphrased)
citation: The Wind in the Willows (1908), chapter 6
text: For stealing a valuable motor car, driving it dangerously and cheeking the police, Mr Toad gets twenty years, the court rounding his total up generously.
summary: Mr Toad, for stealing a valuable motor car, driving it dangerously and evading the police, receives twenty years in prison.

source: Disney, Wreck-It Ralph (paraphrased)
text: Characters who leave their own game risk everything: die in someone else's game and you never regenerate.
summary: Characters who leave their own game risk everything: they die in someone else's game and cannot regenerate.

source: Edicts of the Tokugawa shogunate, 1615-1843 (paraphrased)
text: Every lord must spend every other year in Edo, travelling there and back in a grand and ruinously expensive procession.
summary: Every lord must spend every other year in Edo, traveling there and back in an expensive procession.

source: Edicts of the Tokugawa shogunate, 1615-1843 (paraphrased)
citation: Laws of Compassion for Living Things, Tokugawa Tsunayoshi (1685-1709)
text: Dogs must be treated with respect and never harmed; strays are housed in vast kennels at public expense, which earned the shogun the nickname the Dog Shogun.
summary: Dogs must be treated with respect and never harmed; stray dogs are housed in public kennels.

source: Edicts of the Tokugawa shogunate, 1615-1843 (paraphrased)
text: Townspeople are forbidden luxuries such as fine silk clothing, elaborate hair ornaments and expensive sweets.
summary: Townspeople are forbidden from owning luxuries such as fine silk clothing, elaborate hair ornaments, and expensive sweets.

source: Edicts of the Tokugawa shogunate, 1615-1843 (paraphrased)
text: Warriors must avoid drinking parties and wild revelry, and a lord may not repair his castle without reporting it, still less build a new one.
summary: Warriors must not attend drinking parties or wild revelry, and a lord may not repair or build a castle without reporting it.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: Purple silk and cloth of gold are reserved for the Queen, her family and the highest nobility, and everyone else must dress according to their rank.
summary: Only the Queen, her family and the highest nobility may wear purple silk and cloth of gold; everyone else must dress according to rank.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: Every able-bodied man must practise archery on Sundays and holidays, and may not waste his time on handball, football, cockfighting or other idle games, on pain of prison.
summary: Every able-bodied man must practise archery on Sundays and holidays and may not waste time on idle games, or he will be imprisoned.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: Everyone over six, apart from the nobility and the well-to-do, must wear a woollen cap made in England on Sundays and holy days, or pay three shillings and fourpence, to keep the country's cap makers in work.
summary: Everyone over six, except the nobility and the well-to-do, must wear a woollen cap on Sundays and holy days or pay a fine of three shillings and fourpence.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: The feasts of Christmas, Easter and Whitsun are abolished; instead, scholars, servants and apprentices get one day of recreation a month.
summary: The feasts of Christmas, Easter and Whitsun are abolished; scholars, servants and apprentices receive one day of recreation per month instead.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: No one may lose life or limb for taking the king's deer. A poacher pays a heavy fine, or if he has nothing, spends a year and a day in prison.
summary: No one may kill the king's deer; a poacher must pay a heavy fine or, if he has nothing, serve a year and a day in prison.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: Instead of a whipping or a branding, those convicted of lesser thefts may be transported to the American colonies for seven years, and receivers of stolen goods for fourteen; coming back early is a capital crime.
summary: Those convicted of lesser thefts may be transported to the American colonies for seven years, and receivers of stolen goods for fourteen; early return is a capital crime.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: No one may be served more than two courses at dinner or supper, each of no more than two kinds of food, except on great feast days, when three courses are allowed.
summary: No one may be served more than two courses at dinner or supper, each of no more than two kinds of food, except on great feast days, when three courses are allowed.

source: English statutes, proclamations and charters, 1217-1735 (paraphrased)
text: Pretending to use witchcraft, to tell fortunes or to find lost goods by magic is a fraud punished by a year in prison. The act was last used in 1944, against the medium Helen Duncan.
summary: Pretending to use witchcraft or fortune-telling is fraud punishable by a year in prison.

source: Finland's prohibition law of 1919 (paraphrased)
text: Drinks containing more than two percent alcohol are banned. The ban was repealed in 1932, after a referendum.
summary: Drinks containing more than two percent alcohol are banned.

source: Iceland's prohibition law of 1915 (paraphrased)
text: All alcohol is banned. Wine came back in 1922, so that Spain would keep buying Icelandic fish, and spirits in 1935, but strong beer stayed illegal until 1 March 1989.
summary: All alcohol is banned; wine and spirits were later allowed but strong beer remained illegal until 1 March 1989.

source: Laws of the Massachusetts Bay Colony (paraphrased)
citation: Law of the Massachusetts Bay Colony (1659)
text: Anyone found celebrating Christmas, whether by not working, by feasting or in any other way, pays five shillings for each offence. The law was repealed in 1681.
summary: Anyone celebrating Christmas, whether by not working, feasting or otherwise, must pay five shillings for each offence.
punishment: Fine of five shillings per offence

source: The decrees of Sultan Murad IV (paraphrased)
text: Coffeehouses are closed and coffee, tobacco and wine are banned in Istanbul on pain of death, and the sultan himself patrols the streets in disguise looking for offenders.
summary: Coffeehouses are closed and coffee, tobacco and wine are banned in Istanbul, with death as penalty for offenders.

source: Decrees of Peter the Great, 1698-1718 (paraphrased)
text: Nobles must host and attend assemblies, Western-style evening parties with dancing and conversation; anyone who breaks the rules must drain the Great Eagle, an enormous goblet of vodka.
summary: Nobles must host and attend assemblies; breaking the rules requires draining the Great Eagle, a large vodka goblet.

source: Decrees of Peter the Great, 1698-1718 (paraphrased)
text: A man who wants to keep his beard must pay a yearly beard tax and carry a copper token to prove it; peasants pay a small toll each time they enter a town bearded.
summary: A man who wants to keep his beard must pay a yearly beard tax and carry a copper token; peasants pay a small toll each time they enter a town bearded.
punishment: Pay yearly beard tax and tolls

source: Decrees of Peter the Great, 1698-1718 (paraphrased)
text: Nobles and townspeople must give up long Russian robes for Western-style clothes, and tailors who keep making the old robes are fined.
summary: Nobles and townspeople must abandon long Russian robes for Western-style clothes; tailors who continue making old robes are fined.

source: Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, 1457 and 1491 (paraphrased)
citation: Act of the Parliament of Scotland (1457)
text: Football and golf are to be utterly cried down and not played, so that men practise archery instead, and every parish must keep targets for shooting.
summary: Football and golf are prohibited; men must practice archery instead, and every parish must keep targets for shooting.

source: Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, 1457 and 1491 (paraphrased)
citation: Act of the Parliament of Scotland (1491)
text: No one anywhere in the realm may play football, golf or any other such unprofitable sport, on pain of a fine.
summary: No one may play football, golf or any unprofitable sport, on pain of a fine.

source: Prohibition and Hollywood's Production Code, 1919-1934 (paraphrased)
citation: Eighteenth Amendment (1919) and the Volstead Act
text: Making, selling or transporting intoxicating liquor is forbidden throughout the United States, and anything over half a percent alcohol counts. Repealed in 1933.
summary: Making, selling or transporting intoxicating liquor over half a percent alcohol is forbidden.

source: Prohibition and Hollywood's Production Code, 1919-1934 (paraphrased)
text: Revenge in modern times must never be shown as justified.
summary: Revenge in modern times must never be shown as justified.

source: Prohibition and Hollywood's Production Code, 1919-1934 (paraphrased)
text: The flag must always be treated respectfully on screen.
summary: The flag must always be treated respectfully on screen.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Beating or shaking a carpet, rug or mat in a London street is forbidden, except doormats before eight in the morning.
summary: Beating or shaking a carpet, rug or mat in a London street is forbidden, except doormats before eight in the morning.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Hanging a clothes line across a street is an offence.
summary: Hanging a clothes line across a street is an offence.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Wilfully and wantonly disturbing anyone by ringing a doorbell or knocking at a door without lawful excuse is an offence.
summary: Wilfully and wantonly disturbing anyone by ringing a doorbell or knocking at a door without lawful excuse is an offence.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Being drunk while in charge of a carriage, a horse, cattle or a steam engine on a highway or in any public place is an offence, and it still is.
summary: Being drunk while in charge of a carriage, a horse, cattle or a steam engine on a highway or in any public place is an offence.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Playing football or any other game on a highway, to the annoyance of travellers, costs a fine of up to forty shillings.
summary: Playing football or any other game on a highway, to the annoyance of travellers, costs a fine of up to forty shillings.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Anyone pretending to tell fortunes, or using palmistry or any other subtle craft to deceive, is a rogue and vagabond and may be sent to prison for three months.
summary: Anyone who pretends to tell fortunes or uses palmistry to deceive is considered a rogue and may be imprisoned for three months.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Flying a kite in a London street, to the annoyance of passers-by, is an offence.
summary: Flying a kite in a London street that annoys passers‑by is an offence.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Keeping a pigsty facing the street, unless a proper wall or fence shuts it off, is an offence.
summary: Keeping a pigsty facing the street without a proper wall or fence is an offence.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: A mechanically powered road vehicle needs a crew of at least three, one of whom walks at least sixty yards ahead carrying a red flag to warn riders and drivers of horses.
summary: A mechanically powered road vehicle must have a crew of at least three, one of whom walks at least sixty yards ahead carrying a red flag to warn riders and drivers of horses.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: Making or using a slide on ice or snow in a London street is an offence.
summary: Making or using a slide on ice or snow in a London street is an offence.

source: Acts of Parliament, 1824-1872 (paraphrased)
text: A mechanically powered road vehicle may go no faster than four miles an hour in the country and two miles an hour in towns.
summary: A mechanically powered road vehicle may go no faster than four miles an hour in the country and two miles an hour in towns.

source: The Defence of the Realm Act and its orders, 1914-1918 (paraphrased)
text: Feeding bread to horses, poultry or stray animals is forbidden, to save food for people.
summary: Feeding bread to horses, poultry or stray animals is forbidden to save food for people.

source: The Defence of the Realm Act and its orders, 1914-1918 (paraphrased)
text: Buying a drink for anyone else in a pub is forbidden: everyone pays for their own.
summary: Buying a drink for anyone else in a pub is forbidden; everyone must pay for their own.

source: The Defence of the Realm Act and its orders, 1914-1918 (paraphrased)
citation: Licensing restrictions under the Defence of the Realm Act (1915)
text: Pubs may open only at set hours around lunch and in the evening, and beer is made weaker.
summary: Pubs may open only at set hours around lunch and in the evening, and beer is made weaker.

source: The Defence of the Realm Act and its orders, 1914-1918 (paraphrased)
text: No one may fly a kite or light a bonfire that could signal to the enemy.
summary: No one may fly a kite or light a bonfire that could signal to the enemy.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may fly into a rage without cause.
summary: No one may fly into a rage without cause.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may behave with arrogance or swell with pride.
summary: No one may behave with arrogance or swell with pride.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may encroach on another person's fields or move the markers that mark them.
summary: No one may encroach on another person's fields or move the markers that mark them.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may carry off the cakes offered to the spirits of the dead.
summary: No one may carry off the cakes offered to the spirits of the dead.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may talk more than is needed, or raise their voice without reason.
summary: No one may talk more than is needed, or raise their voice without reason.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may eavesdrop.
summary: No one may eavesdrop.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may tell lies.
summary: No one may tell lies.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may tamper with the scales or give short measure of grain.
summary: The law forbids tampering with the scales or giving a short measure of grain, and if done, the offender must face unspecified consequences.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: Before the forty-two judges of the dead, everyone must be able to swear that they have never stolen.
summary: The law requires everyone to swear before the forty-two judges of the dead that they have never stolen, and failure to do so results in unspecified consequences.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may cause another person to weep.
summary: The law forbids causing another person to weep, and violation leads to unspecified consequences.

source: The Book of the Dead, chapter 125, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1895) (paraphrased)
text: No one may hold back the floodwater in its season, or dam a running stream that others need.
summary: The law prohibits holding back floodwater in its season or damming a running stream needed by others, with unspecified penalties for violation.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: A mortal who boasts she is better than a goddess, and proves it, may be turned into a spider: Arachne out-wove Athena and was changed into one, to spin forever.
summary: The law states that a mortal who boasts of being better than a goddess and proves it may be turned into a spider, as Arachne was turned into a spider after out-woven Athena.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: Whoever cuts down a grove sacred to Demeter is punished with endless hunger: Erysichthon ate everything he owned and was never full.
summary: The law declares that cutting down a grove sacred to Demeter results in endless hunger, as Erysichthon was punished by never being full.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: When the newborn Hermes stole fifty of Apollo's cattle, Zeus ordered him to show where they were hidden, and Hermes settled the matter by giving Apollo the lyre he had invented.
summary: The law says that if a newborn Hermes steals fifty of Apollo's cattle, Zeus orders him to show where they were hidden, and Hermes settles by giving Apollo the lyre he invented.
punishment: Return of cattle and giving of lyre

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: A soul released from the underworld must follow you out, and you may not look back until you both reach the light. Orpheus looked back, and lost Eurydice forever.
summary: The law requires a soul released from the underworld to follow you out and not look back until both reach the light, and if you look back, you lose the soul forever, as Orpheus lost Eurydice.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: Whoever eats the food of the underworld must stay there. Persephone ate a few pomegranate seeds, and so spends part of every year below.
summary: Eating underworld food forces the eater to remain there for part of each year.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: A king who cheats death must push a boulder up a hill for eternity, only for it to roll back down every time.
summary: Cheating death requires the king to eternally push a boulder uphill only for it to roll back down.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: A god who swears by the water of the Styx and then breaks the oath lies breathless and speechless for a year, then is shut out of the gods' councils and feasts for nine more.
summary: A god who swears by Styx water and breaks the oath becomes breathless and speechless for a year, then is excluded from councils and feasts for nine more.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: Tantalus stole nectar and ambrosia from the gods' table to share with his friends, and now stands forever in water he cannot drink, beneath fruit he cannot reach.
summary: Stealing nectar and ambrosia causes the thief to forever stand in unattainable water and fruit.

source: Greek myths, retold from Hesiod, Homer, Pindar and Ovid (paraphrased)
text: Strangers and beggars are under the protection of Zeus, god of guests: a host must feed and shelter them before asking who they are, and harming a guest is among the worst crimes there is.
summary: Hosts must feed and shelter strangers and beggars before questioning them, and harming a guest is a severe crime.

source: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West (16th century) (paraphrased)
text: A disciple who disobeys his master wears a golden headband that tightens whenever the master recites a certain spell.
summary: Disobeying a master causes a disciple to wear a tightening golden headband whenever the master recites a spell.

source: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West (16th century) (paraphrased)
text: Stealing the Peaches of Immortality from the Queen Mother's garden and gatecrashing her banquet earns five hundred years trapped beneath a mountain: the sentence of the Monkey King.
summary: Stealing the Peaches of Immortality and gatecrashing the Queen Mother's banquet results in five hundred years trapped beneath a mountain.

jurisdiction_name: Yomi, the land of the dead
source: The Kojiki (712), trans. B. H. Chamberlain (1882) (paraphrased)
text: When you visit the dead, do not look at them: Izanagi lit a torch to look at Izanami in the underworld, and she chased him out in fury.
summary: Looking at the dead during a visit causes the visitor to be chased out in fury.

jurisdiction_name: Takamagahara, the High Plain of Heaven
source: The Kojiki (712), trans. B. H. Chamberlain (1882) (paraphrased)
text: After Susanoo wrecked Amaterasu's rice fields and defiled her weaving hall, the gods fined him a thousand tables of offerings, cut off his beard and nails, and banished him from heaven.
summary: After defiling Amaterasu's fields, Susanoo is fined a thousand tables of offerings, has his beard and nails cut, and is banished from heaven.
punishment: Fine of a thousand tables; beard and nails cut; banishment

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: Ale is not as good as people say: the more a man drinks, the less he knows.
summary: The law says that the more a man drinks ale, the less he knows.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: A man should not boast of his wits but keep watch over his words: the wise and silent rarely come to harm.
summary: A man should not boast of his wits but keep watch over his words; the wise and silent rarely come to harm.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: Rise early if you want another man's goods: a wolf that lies asleep gets no meat.
summary: The law says that if you want another man's goods, you must rise early; a wolf that lies asleep gets no meat.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: A greedy man eats himself into misery. Even cattle know when to leave the pasture, but a glutton never knows the measure of his stomach.
summary: The law says that a greedy man eats himself into misery and never knows the measure of his stomach.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: A guest must leave in good time: even a friend becomes a burden if he sits too long in another man's hall.
summary: The law says that a guest must leave in good time, or he becomes a burden if he sits too long in another man's hall.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: A fool who keeps quiet may pass for wise, until he talks too much.
summary: The law says that a fool who keeps quiet may pass for wise until he talks too much.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: Never mock a guest or drive a stranger from your door, and treat the wretched kindly.
summary: The law says that you should never mock a guest or drive a stranger from your door, and treat the wretched kindly.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: When a giant steals Thor's hammer and holds it for ransom, Thor must go to the giant's feast in disguise, eat a whole ox and eight salmon, and take his hammer back.
summary: The law says that when a giant steals Thor's hammer and holds it for ransom, Thor must go to the giant's feast in disguise, eat a whole ox and eight salmon, and take his hammer back.

source: The Poetic Edda, trans. H. A. Bellows (1923) (paraphrased)
text: A traveller arriving from a cold journey needs fire, food, dry clothes and water, and a friendly welcome.
summary: The law says that a traveller arriving from a cold journey needs fire, food, dry clothes and water, and a friendly welcome.

source: The Ulster Cycle, as told in Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) (paraphrased)
text: A hero bound by a geis must never break it. Cuchulain was sworn never to eat dog meat and never to refuse a meal offered at a hearth; offered dog meat, he had to break one, and his strength left him.
summary: A hero bound by a geis must never break it; if he does, he loses his strength.

source: The Japanese folk tale of Urashima Taro (paraphrased)
text: A box given as a parting gift by the Dragon Palace must never be opened: Urashima Taro opened his and aged three hundred years in a moment.
summary: A box given as a parting gift by the Dragon Palace must never be opened; opening it causes the owner to age rapidly.
